In this essay
  1. I. One Run, Two Numbers
  2. II. An Average for a Particular Position
  3. III. The Numbers That Scatter
  4. IV. Why Hand Times Are Always Rounded Up
  5. V. Thousandths Stay Inside
  6. VI. Not Conversion, but Elevation to Official Status
  7. VII. One Thread, Two Pieces of Cloth
  8. VIII. Hand Timing Is Still Legal; It Just No Longer Counts

I. One Run, Two Numbers

In the subsequent progression of records, the hundred metres Hines ran in Mexico City in 1968 carries two numbers.

One is 9.9 seconds, hand-timed. The other is 9.95 seconds, fully automatically timed.

This was the same run. Not two races, not two people, but the same hundred metres that Hines completed on that track that day. Two systems were timing it simultaneously: one operated by a person's hand, the other triggered by a machine. They produced two numbers.

The same was true of Smith's two hundred metres: 19.8 and 19.83. And of Evans's four hundred metres: 43.8 and 43.86. In each case, one run, two numbers.

It looks like a small matter. One is recorded to a tenth, the other to a hundredth, as though the difference were simply precision. But it is not. 9.9 and 9.95 are not two ways of writing the same number, one coarse and one fine. They are two different results produced by two different measuring systems observing the same event.

This point must be established first, because everything that follows grows out of it. For a number to mean anything, we must first know what measured it. 9.9 and 9.95 differ not because one is wrong, but because one was produced by a human finger and the other triggered by an electronic circuit. A finger and a circuit do not apprehend the same instant in the same way. The question of how fast Hines actually ran therefore has no answer independent of the method of measurement. He ran 9.9, and he ran 9.95, depending on which system you listen to.

The previous essay ended with two ledgers. The official record table does not distinguish altitude, while statisticians privately maintain a low-altitude list. Both coexist, and the official one never acknowledges the other. Those were two ledgers of altitude. This essay concerns two ledgers of timing, a more fundamental division because it lies inside the number that constitutes the performance itself. Hines's run belongs simultaneously to two ledgers, under two numbers.

The problem is that the record table can contain only one number.

Something was therefore needed to connect the two ledgers. That something was a constant: 0.24 seconds.

II. An Average for a Particular Position

Where did the number 0.24 come from?

Later athletics literature consistently traces it to a study of expert hand timers associated with the 1972 Munich Olympics and the University of Giessen. The best available overview says the study found an average difference of approximately 0.18 seconds between hand and automatic timing when the timer or starter was close to the starting pistol; approximately 0.24 seconds on the hundred-metre straight; and approximately 0.26 seconds on the two-hundred-metre bend.

The most important point is concealed in those three numbers.

0.24 is not a universal constant. It is an average for a particular geometrical arrangement. With the timer at the finish of the hundred-metre straight, the average difference is 0.24; at the far end of the two-hundred-metre bend, 0.26; close to the pistol, 0.18. Change the position and the number changes.

In other words, from the moment it came into being, this constant was not a constant at all, but one value of a quantity that varies with position. People subsequently selected one of those values, 0.24, and made it the constant.

The selected value happens to lie between the other two: 0.18 near the pistol, 0.26 on the bend, and 0.24 in between. But 0.24 also corresponds to the particular straight-hundred-metre arrangement described above. Its position in the middle does not establish that it was chosen as a compromise. The real question is transfer. Each race has its own starting arrangements, timer positions and human responses. Fixing an average from one set of conditions makes different results easier to connect; it does not guarantee the right correction for every individual observation.

And its being an average has a further, more important implication.

An average is calculated from a set of numbers. Some are greater than 0.24, others smaller. The average does not describe any one of those individual numbers. It describes their centre. Using an average as a constant means substituting the centre of the set for every member of it, when the members were originally dispersed.

How widely those numbers were dispersed is the crucial question in this essay, and in this round of research no direct answer was available. The original papers from the 1970s directly examined did not yield the sample size, full distribution, or standard deviation of the Munich–Giessen study. Later accounts describe the figures as averages, but provide no original tables, sample counts, standard deviations, or confidence intervals. Nor do they specify clearly whether the published statistic was a mean or an average aggregated by condition.

What can therefore be established is that 0.24 is an average for a particular position. What cannot be established is how widely dispersed the numbers that generated it originally were.

That gap is not trivial. Whether an average is useful depends on how widely the underlying numbers are dispersed. If they are clustered tightly around 0.24, substituting 0.24 for each produces little error. If they are widely scattered, 0.24 will be inaccurate for many of them. And precisely the information that would determine its accuracy is unavailable today.

III. The Numbers That Scatter

The original paper is unavailable, but later studies have measured similar things, and those studies reveal the extent of the scatter.

In a study of eighty-one US college football players running forty-yard sprints, the mean difference between hand and electronic times was 0.22 seconds for experienced timers, with a standard deviation of 0.07 seconds. For inexperienced timers, those figures were 0.26 and 0.08 seconds. Electronic timing began when the athlete's hand left a ground touchpad and ended at an infrared beam. This was not the same arrangement as gun-started fully automatic timing for the hundred metres.

Look first at the two averages, 0.22 and 0.26. Both fall close to 0.24. This seems to support 0.24 as a reasonable number.

Now look at the two standard deviations, 0.07 and 0.08. They remind us that an average difference does not eliminate variation.

A standard deviation of 0.07 does not confine all differences to the interval from 0.15 to 0.29. Those are merely the positions one standard deviation below and above the mean; observations can fall outside them. Under this study's conditions, adding the same average to every hand time would not remove each individual error. In a closely contested hundred metres, 0.15 seconds can separate gold from a finish well away from the podium. That illustrates the importance of small margins; it does not turn this forty-yard study into an error bound for every hundred-metre race.

The question becomes clearer in its historical setting. Many gold and silver medals have been separated by less than a tenth of a second; small margins deserve serious attention. But this study does not establish a universal 0.15-second threshold for hundred-metre performances. How much a small gap between two converted times tells us depends on the original timing conditions, errors and comparability. The average correction alone cannot certify a ranking to the hundredth. The constant can stitch two pieces of cloth together; the seam alone cannot guarantee a ranking to the hundredth.

The study establishes at least this much: a mean difference measured under particular conditions can describe that set of observations without supplying the exact correction for each one. Without a fuller independent record of a particular race, the mean alone cannot tell us its error. Nor does this validate a constant from another period and another timing arrangement.

A structure shared with the previous essay appears here, and deserves a brief mention.

With Beamon's jump, the problem was that four variables combined into one number could not be disentangled afterward. Here the problem runs in reverse: after an average is applied to every individual, we cannot tell whether it fits this particular one. In the former case, several causes combine into one result and cannot be separated; in the latter, one average stands in for many individuals and cannot be verified. Both concern the construct's way of handling uncertainty. In both, it accepts something unverifiable so that the ledger can keep being written.

We can put this more generally, because it recurs throughout the series. A construct that keeps accounts over time will sooner or later encounter uncertainty it cannot eliminate. It can take one of two positions. It can stop, refusing to record anything uncertain, in which case it will record very little. Or it can accept an unverifiable procedure, compress uncertainty into a number or a constant, and continue. Almost every construct capable of sustained operation chooses the latter. The price is that every number in its ledger seals within it a little something that the construct itself cannot verify.

Another popular claim about the constant is that hand timing is always 0.24 seconds faster than electronic timing. This is false. A hand time can be faster or slower, depending on the timer's behaviour, training, anticipation, and the geometry of the track. The historical constant is an average adjustment, not a mechanical truth about every race. A statistician with long experience in the field explicitly identifies the universal “0.24 faster” story as a misconception, while acknowledging that 0.24 is broadly serviceable as an average convention for well-trained timers.

Both statements must be made together. The constant is usable as a convention and unreliable as a description of an individual case. It is both at once, which is precisely why it continues to be used and continues to be questioned.

IV. Why Hand Times Are Always Rounded Up

Something else widens the difference between hand and electronic timing, and it is often overlooked.

The rounding rule for hand timing is upward rounding, not rounding to the nearest value.

In the accessible IAAF rules, hand-timed track performances are read to the next longer tenth of a second. If the watch measures hundredths, or a manually operated digital timer is used, any performance whose second decimal place is not zero must be rounded to the next longer tenth. For example, 10.11 becomes 10.2.

The rule means that hand times are always adjusted in the slower direction. 10.11 is plainly closer to 10.1, yet it is written as 10.2. This is not rounding to the nearest value. It only rounds upward, never down.

The rule has an easily overlooked consequence. By the time a hand-timed performance is written down, it has already undergone an adjustment toward a slower time, before any conversion takes place. Thus, when people say hand timing is 0.24 seconds faster than electronic timing, the hand time being compared is already a number rounded in the slower direction. Another upward rounding separates the actual reading produced by the timer's finger from the number finally entered on the results sheet. This frequently overlooked layer makes the real difference between hand and electronic timing more complicated than it appears.

Why do this? Hand timing is affected by responses to the start and judgments at the finish. Some studies and conversion conventions address hand times that are faster on average. But starting early and stopping late would lengthen a recorded time, not shorten it. Upward rounding specifies how a reading is reported, always toward the slower value. The rule alone does not establish that it was designed to compensate for one particular response bias.

Where this 0.24-second conversion is used, two procedures are superimposed on a hand time. The first is upward rounding, making it slower. The second is the constant of 0.24, adding another stretch of time. Both act in the same direction, bringing the hand-timed number closer to the electronic one.

Electronic times are also rounded upward, but to a finer unit. Current rules require track performances over distances up to and including 10,000 metres to be read, converted, and recorded to the next longer hundredth of a second unless already exact. Track races longer than 10,000 metres are recorded to the next longer tenth; road races to the next longer whole second.

Taken together, these rules reveal a consistent approach to rounding within the construct: it would rather make a performance look slightly slower than slightly faster. Every rounding goes upward, toward slower times.

There is a reason for this, connected to the nature of the record as a construct. Once a record is ratified, it becomes the benchmark everyone afterward must surpass. If rounding makes a record appear faster than it really was, subsequent athletes face an artificially high target. That is unfair to them. Conversely, if rounding makes it appear slightly slower, at worst it disadvantages the present athlete rather than everyone who follows.

Confronted with the unavoidable choice of how to round, the construct therefore chooses to place the error on the present individual rather than on all future individuals. This is a deliberate bias toward continuity of the ledger, not accuracy of the current performance.

Behind that choice lies an asymmetrical judgment about fairness. Disadvantaging the current individual harms one person, once. Making everyone afterward face an artificially high benchmark harms many people, many times. Weighing the two harms, the construct concentrates the injury on the one to protect the many who follow. The choice is defensible, but it is not neutral. Between present and future athletes, it systematically takes the future's side. Taking the future's side means taking the ledger's side, because the ledger is written for the future.

V. Thousandths Stay Inside

Modern timing systems use thousandths of a second internally, but thousandths are not the official precision of records.

The accessible World Athletics rules separately specify photo-finish sampling requirements and a constant delay of no more than one millisecond between the starting signal and activation of the timing system. That trigger delay is neither the system's resolution nor a bound on its total measurement error; these are different technical quantities. Published results, however, are still read to a hundredth or a tenth, depending on the length of the event.

There is something strange here. The construct can measure to a thousandth, yet chooses to publish only hundredths. It withholds part of its precision inside the system.

Why not use thousandths as the precision for records? No original provision explaining this could be found in the accessible rules. They specify that it is not done, without explaining why. The practical reasons are almost certainly standardisation and historical continuity, but those reasons are not explicitly stated in the verifiable original text.

The shape of the decision itself is nevertheless clear, and connects with the preceding essays.

The precision a construct publishes is not the greatest precision it can achieve, but the precision it chooses to take responsibility for. Measuring to thousandths and publishing hundredths means deliberately relinquishing the intervening digit. There is an obvious benefit: hundredths remain compatible with several preceding decades of performances.

Here we can see a general principle. Once a measuring system is established, greater precision is not necessarily better. It must remain compatible with its own history. For an isolated measurement, greater precision is of course preferable. But a measurement intended for comparison with decades of older data opens an unbridgeable gap with those data if its precision suddenly increases by one order. The construct's own past thus locks its precision in place. It cannot raise the precision of published results whenever technology advances, because every additional digit invalidates another degree of historical comparability. Hines's 9.95 in 1968 was measured to a hundredth. If thousandths were now adopted, every previous record written in hundredths would face an awkward situation: its next digit is unknown, whereas the new performances have one. A new incomparability would emerge.

The construct therefore prefers to forgo that digit in order to preserve comparison with the past. Its choice is the same as the choice concerning altitude in Essay Five: to maintain continuity within a single table, it deliberately relinquishes some accuracy that could otherwise be available. Precision and continuity cannot both be maximised. It chooses continuity.

The thousandths have not disappeared. They remain inside the system, used when necessary to determine places. The construct thus uses its highest available precision for placings, and a coarser, historically compatible precision for records. One precision decides who wins; another writes the ledger. The coexistence of these two precisions is yet another instance of two ledgers.

VI. Not Conversion, but Elevation to Official Status

In 1976 the IAAF agreed that only automatically timed sprint performances would be accepted as world records, effective from 1 January 1977.

The easiest misunderstanding is to imagine that the construct took the old hand-timed records, added 0.24, and converted them into electronic equivalents.

It did not.

After the transition, the treatment of older performances fell into three categories. First, where a fully automatic time already existed for the same race, that electronic reading was retained as the automatic benchmark. Second, where the event still qualified for hand timing, the performance remained a hand-timed or automatically timed record. Third, where the event itself was abolished, it was removed from record eligibility.

Consider the first category, which makes the point most clearly.

For Hines's hundred metres, the old hand-timed list continued to use the pre-1977 mark of 9.9. But once a separate automatically timed list existed, it recorded the 9.95 Hines ran in Mexico City on 14 October 1968 as the electronic record, noting that automatic timing to hundredths became mandatory on 1 January 1977.

The construct was therefore not adding 0.24 to 9.9 to turn it into 9.95. It was elevating to official status the 9.95 that had existed at the time of the same race.

The distinction matters. 9.95 was not calculated from 9.9. It was there already. Two systems timed Hines's run at the time: the hand-timing system supplied 9.9, the electronic system 9.95. In 1977 the construct declared that the electronic system would henceforth be authoritative. The 9.95 that had always existed but had not previously been official became official.

Smith's two hundred metres and Evans's four hundred were treated in exactly the same way. 19.83 was already there; 43.86 was already there. The construct did not convert the old ledger. It elevated a long-coexisting number beside that ledger, then invalidated the column to which the old entry belonged.

This has the same structure as the observation in Essay Two: the first thing the construct learned was how to add; it was never taught to subtract. Here, too, it did not change the old number into a new number, which would have required subtraction followed by addition. It raised the status of an existing number while invalidating the entire column containing the old one. Once again, it acknowledged something already there rather than erasing one thing and replacing it with another.

These practices suggest a preference: alter the ledger through recognition of an existing reading or a change of eligibility, rather than describe every alteration as a repudiation of the old account. The early authorising provision quoted in Essay Two speaks of registration. That sentence alone cannot establish that no power of cancellation developed later. Recognising an existing number is registration; promoting it to official status is registration; making an old column ineligible can remove a category from current comparison. In these examples, changing the ledger need not always mean declaring that the past was recorded wrongly. This does not establish that the institution lacked other powers.

We must identify what remains unavailable. An exhaustive administrative list specifying the precise legal disposition of every pre-1977 sprint, hurdle, and relay record would require direct consultation of IAAF record books or congress proceedings from those years. Available material clearly establishes the pattern and provides prominent examples, but not an official consolidated disposition table. The pattern is therefore established; the item-by-item treatment could not be fully recovered in this round of research.

Non-metric sprint and hurdle events were treated differently again: they were removed from the record lists rather than converted. World Athletics' historical page says that the 1976 decision removed imperial events other than the mile. They were not converted into metric equivalents. They simply disappeared from the ledger. Essay Seven will address this kind of deletion specifically.

VII. One Thread, Two Pieces of Cloth

We can now return the constant of 0.24 to its proper place and see it clearly.

It is a stitching thread.

Hand timing is one piece of cloth; electronic timing another. They were woven on different machines, with different warps and wefts. The smallest square in one is a tenth of a second, in the other a hundredth. But the construct needs a complete table, joining the two pieces together. 0.24 is the thread that stitches them.

A stitching thread has a particular property: it is strong overall but loose at each stitch. A thread of 0.24 on average can align the two pieces approximately, making a reasonably presentable table. At each individual stitch, however, it cannot accurately establish which point on the electronic cloth corresponds to a particular hand time. It may miss by 0.05 on one side or 0.05 on the other. Overall alignment, local misalignment.

This property belongs to every practice that uses averages to handle individuals. A table made for the average body suits the population as a whole but not a particularly tall or short person. A conversion constant based on the average difference aligns a batch of timings but misaligns an individual timing. The only difference is that the table's misfit is immediately visible, whereas the timing misfit is invisible, because there is no true electronic reading for that athlete against which to check it. Invisible misalignment is more dangerous than visible misalignment, because it is taken for the absence of misalignment.

That is why the constant continues to be used and continues to be criticised.

Its critics say a fixed constant is often too crude for real populations of timers. One observer compared electronic times with nominal backup hand times at local high-school finals and found average gaps of 0.40–0.45 seconds, much larger than 0.24. He argued that using 0.24 in such settings materially distorts qualification and seeding. This was not a peer-reviewed athletics-journal study, but an empirical criticism by a direct observer with long experience in statistics and commentary.

Its defenders say fixed constants remain defensible for well-trained timers and for the administrative comparability required by systems that still have to rank hand and electronic times together. This is the logic embedded in ranking systems, combined-events conversions, and long-established academic guidelines.

Both sides are in fact right, but about different things.

Understanding what each side is right about is the destination of this essay, because it takes us closer to the truth than choosing a side. Many disputes about measurement appear to pit claims of accuracy against claims of inaccuracy. In fact, one side is speaking about aggregates and the other about individuals, and both claims can be true. 0.24 is usable overall and unreliable individually. That is not a contradiction waiting to be resolved. It is the normal condition of applying averages to individuals. Acknowledging that condition is more honest than insisting that the constant must be either reliable or unreliable.

The defenders are right that, as a means of stitching two pieces of cloth together, 0.24 is broadly usable. The construct genuinely needs such a means, or the two pieces cannot form one table. The critics are right that the thread is inaccurate at each stitch, and may be very far off when the timers' competence departs from that of the expert population that originally produced the average.

A fair conclusion is that the constant retains institutional usefulness but offers weak precision for individuals. It is a thread that holds firmly overall and loosely in particular places. Both properties are real.

The construct's subsequent practical response deserves attention. It did not issue an official document specifically defending or revising the constant. Its actual response was different: require fully automatic timing for more records, require certified start-information systems, and largely leave conversion formulas to national, academic, ranking, and combined-events settings rather than the central process of world-record ratification.

In other words, instead of improving the stitching thread, the construct made its central table need as little stitching as possible. Core records recognise only electronic timing: one piece of cloth, no seam required. The thread survives at the edges, wherever two pieces must still be joined. This repeats the previous essay's pattern: faced with a problem it cannot fully solve, the construct moves it to the periphery so that its core no longer has to encounter it.

VIII. Hand Timing Is Still Legal; It Just No Longer Counts

Today hand timing remains legal under World Athletics rules, one of the recognised official timing methods.

Current rules recognise three methods: hand timing, fully automatic timing obtained from a photo-finish system, and transponder timing. Hand timing has therefore not lost its legitimacy as a way of producing an official result. It remains valid in competitions that do not require fully automatic timing, or as a backup where fully automatic timing is used.

What hand timing lost was not legality, but equal standing in record ratification for shorter events. Current rules require fully automatic timing for records in events up to and including eight hundred metres.

This situation deserves a pause, because it is characteristic of the construct's treatment of something old.

It did not abolish hand timing. Abolition would have required a decision, a written provision, and a confrontation with all the lower-level competitions still using it. Instead, it preserved hand timing's legality while stripping it of eligibility for the most important purpose. Hand timing remains. It can produce an official result, but that result cannot enter the short-event record table.

This is the same manoeuvre as the fate of the word “amateur” in Essay Three. Amateurism was not declared abolished on a particular day; a new definition hollowed it out. An amateur was someone who obeyed the rules, and the word ceased to refer to anything outside them. Hand timing, too, was not abolished. It was stripped of record eligibility, leaving it to count only where less was at stake. When the construct wants to relinquish something, it seldom cuts it off directly. More often it empties it of power, allowing it to remain without letting it do the work it once did.

This hollowing-out is more effective than direct abolition because it provokes almost no resistance. Abolishing hand timing would immediately affect every lower-level competition dependent on it, giving each a reason to object. Merely removing record eligibility leaves those competitions free to continue as before. Unaffected, they have no reason to object. Top-level competitions that actually care about records can already afford electronic timing, and do not object either. The construct quietly changes the status of hand timing without provoking strong opposition from either side. Emptying something of power often meets far less resistance than abolishing it, because each particular person feels personally unaffected.

And the stitching thread, 0.24, remains in institutional use today.

USA Track & Field still instructs combined-events users to add 0.24 to hand times for events shorter than four hundred metres, and 0.14 for four hundred metres. Its youth-entry guidance still explains how hand-timed qualifying marks relate to fully automatic standards, using 0.24, 0.14, or no addition depending on distance. The National Federation of State High School Associations still publishes a 0.24 hand-to-fully-automatic conversion rule.

The two numbers, 0.24 and 0.14, are therefore still stitching. They no longer stitch the central world-record table, but the peripheral tables in which hand and automatic times must coexist: qualification, seeding, rankings, combined events. The central table is now one piece of cloth. These peripheral tables still join two pieces and still need the thread.

Return to Hines's run.

9.9 and 9.95: two numbers for the same run. The construct eventually chose 9.95, relegating the hand-timed 9.9 to an old list that gradually lost eligibility as event rules changed. That choice did not deliver a perfectly error-free elapsed time; a machine, too, supplies a reading within a measurement system. This does not deny that fully automatic timing can improve accuracy. There is also an institutional decision: from a particular point onward, which system's readings will be used consistently as the official basis of comparison?

This was not only a matter of measuring more accurately. It was also the selection of a shared standard.

In the previous essay, a performance's causes could not be separated. In this one, its numerical value depends on the cloth used to measure it. Together they say the same thing: every number recorded by the construct is not the event itself, but an imprint left in the ledger after the event has passed through a particular apparatus, a particular constant, a particular rounding operation, and a particular chosen standard. The imprint is accurate, checkable, comparable. None of the things separating it from the event enters the ledger.

This is where the first six essays can be gathered together. The construct began with an ancient list containing names alone and gradually built ever more precise means of measurement: newspapers, stopwatches, electronic timing, photo finishes. Each advance made what it recorded a little more accurate. Yet however accurate it became, it still recorded an imprint, not the event. The name is not the person. 9.95 records the duration of Hines's run; it does not contain the whole event. 8.90 metres is not the full set of causes of Beamon's jump. The more precise the construct becomes, the clearer the imprint. But the gap between imprint and event remains, growing finer and finer until it is almost invisible, and people suppose it has disappeared. It has always been there.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 前一篇讲过，这个构记下的每一个数，都不是那件事本身，是那件事经过某一套装置之后留在账簿上的印子。海因斯那一跑，九秒九还是九秒九五，取决于用哪块布来量。这一篇讲的是一个更彻底的版本。十项全能的总分，不是取决于用哪块布来量某一个成绩，而是取决于用哪一张表，把十个互不相干的成绩换算到同一个数上，然后加起来。而这张表，被改过五次。
edits.after: 前一篇讲过，这个构记下的每一个数，都不是那件事本身，是那件事经过某一套装置之后留在账簿上的印子。海因斯那一跑，九秒九还是九秒九五，取决于用哪块布来量。这一篇讲的是一个更彻底的版本。十项全能的总分，不是取决于用哪块布来量某一个成绩，而是取决于用哪一张表，把十个互不相干的成绩换算到同一个数上，然后加起来。而这张表，曾多次修订。上面选了五个版本来比较，并不是列出了全部修订。

edits.before: 值得先注意一件事，这五个总分之间的差距有多大。八千四百一十二和六千二百六十七之间，差了两千一百多分。在十项全能里，这是一个能把奥运冠军和一个入不了决赛的选手分开的差距。而这个差距，不是两个运动员之间的，是同一个运动员的同一场比赛，在两张表下的。换句话说，选用哪张表所带来的分数变化，比许多运动员之间的真实差距还要大。汇率的选择，盖过了成绩本身。
edits.after: 值得先注意这五个总分之间的数字差距：八千四百一十二和六千二百六十七，相差两千一百多分。它们不是两名运动员在同一张表下的分差，不能直接套成冠军与另一名选手之间的竞技差距；十项全能也不是先取得决赛资格再争冠军的赛制。这里显出的，是同一个人的同一场比赛，换了计分尺度就会换一个总数。成绩没有重做，账面上的大小却明显变了。

edits.before: 跳高九百五十八分意味着什么，值得换算一下。1912年那张表把每个项目的1908年奥运纪录定为一千分。索普的跳高一米八七能得九百五十八分，说明这个成绩在那张线性表下，已经非常接近当时奥运纪录的水平了。同一个一米八七，在现行表下只值六百八十七分，不是因为一米八七这个高度变矮了，是因为现行表把跳高这个项目在整个十项里的估价压低了，同样接近纪录的成绩，换到的分数少了。成绩没动，它在总盘子里的分量被调小了。
edits.after: 跳高九百五十八分意味着什么，值得换算一下。1912年那张表把每个项目的1908年奥运纪录定为一千分。索普的跳高一米八七能得九百五十八分，说明这个成绩在那张线性表下，已经非常接近当时奥运纪录的水平了。同一个一米八七，在现行表下只值六百八十七分，不是因为一米八七这个高度变矮了，是因为计分基准和换算方式已经改变。同样是一米八七，在1912年接近当时奥运纪录，并不意味着今天也同样接近纪录。这里能直接看见的是：成绩没动，换到的分数少了；只凭这一点，还不能断定跳高在所有水平上相对其他项目都被调低了。

edits.before: 索普强在跳高和栏，而现行表恰恰调低了跳高和栏的估价，所以他的总分整体是跌的。一个在铅球和铁饼上强的运动员，换到现行表下可能是涨的。表的每一次重写，都在悄悄地改变历史上哪些十项全能选手更值钱。
edits.after: 在索普这组成绩里，跳高和栏换到现行表后都少了分，总分也下降了。另一种成绩组合的变化未必相同；它要看十项各自的实际成绩和新旧曲线，不能只凭擅长哪一项就下结论。表的重写因此可能改变跨时代比较里不同类型选手的相对位置。

edits.before: 这件事有一个让人不安的推论。一个运动员职业生涯结束的时候，他以为自己知道自己站在历史上的什么位置，因为他有一个总分，这个总分可以和前人后人比。可是这个位置不是固定的。若干年后表一改，他的总分和所有人的总分一起被重算，他在历史序列里的排名可能上升，也可能下降，而他本人对此无能为力，甚至可能已经不在人世。一个人一生的努力被压缩成的那个数，不是他能锁定的，它掌握在后来那些改表的人手里。
edits.after: 这件事有一个让人不安的推论。一个运动员职业生涯结束的时候，他以为自己知道自己站在历史上的什么位置，因为他有一个总分，这个总分可以和前人后人比。可是这个位置不是固定的。若干年后，若用新表对旧成绩作跨代重算，他和其他人的比较分都会变化，在这个重算序列里的位置可能上升，也可能下降；这不等于原赛事的奖牌和正式结果自动改判，而他本人也无法决定后来采用哪种比较尺度，甚至可能已经不在人世。一个人一生的努力被压缩成的那个数，不是他能锁定的，它掌握在后来那些改表的人手里。

edits.before: 这三种答案没有一个是错的，因为它们回答的根本不是一个事实问题，是一个政策问题:这项运动想奖励什么。想奖励雨露均沾的全面，还是想奖励在某一项上逼近人类极限的突破，不同的答案通向不同的表形状。这个构在三十年里换了三次立场，而每一次换立场，所有历史成绩的总分排序都跟着变一次。
edits.after: 这三种答案没有一个是错的，因为它们回答的根本不是一个事实问题，是一个政策问题:这项运动想奖励什么。想奖励雨露均沾的全面，还是想奖励在某一项上逼近人类极限的突破，不同的答案通向不同的表形状。这个构在三十年里换了三次立场，而每一次换立场，若据此重算旧成绩，跨代比较中的总分和排序就可能变化；这和改判原比赛是两件事。

edits.before: 一张统治着这项运动的表，它的每一个数字都公开，任何人都能拿来用，算出精确到个位的分数。而这些数字是根据什么定出来的，不公开，或者说，从来没有被完整地写下来过。所以这个构处在一个位置上:它执行着一套精确的规则，而这套规则的来源它自己也讲不清楚。
edits.after: 一张统治着这项运动的表，它的每一个数字都公开，任何人都能拿来用，算出精确到个位的分数。而这些数字怎样一步步定出来，在这里查到的公开材料中，还不能完整复建。不能因此断定当时从未写过，或者机构内部也无人知道；这里留下的问题是，公众可以精确执行这套规则，却未必能从现有公开资料完整重走它的制定过程。

edits.before: 这和第三篇里那件事是相通的。业余原则曾经用一段不存在的古代来为自己辩护，而那段古代是假的这件事，一天也没有减弱过它的效力。这里的情况类似而更微妙:计分系数没有一个假的来源，它是根本没有一个被写下来的来源。它照样精确地运行，照样决定每一场十项全能的胜负，照样把索普的撑竿跳从七百五十分改成四百分。一个构的规则可以精确到不容争辩，同时它为什么是这些数字而不是别的数字，没有人能完整地回答。
edits.after: 这和第三篇里那件事是相通的。业余原则曾经用一段不存在的古代来为自己辩护，而那段古代是假的这件事，一天也没有减弱过它的效力。这里的情况类似而更微妙:计分系数这里的问题，不是揭出了一个假的来源，而是在这里可得的公开材料中，还缺少一个可以完整追溯的推导。它照样精确地运行，照样决定每一场十项全能的胜负，照样把索普的撑竿跳从七百五十分改成四百分。一个构的规则可以精确到不容争辩，同时它为什么是这些数字而不是别的数字，本文尚不能根据这些材料完整回答。

edits.before: 北欧两项也是这样。它把跳台滑雪的分数，通过贡德森方法换算成越野滑雪的出发延迟。个人的五到十五公里比赛，官方的换算是每一分对应四秒。同样，比赛以第一个冲线结束，而不是以一堆异质的子分数的最终加总结束。
edits.after: 北欧两项的个人贡德森赛制也有类似办法：把跳台滑雪的分差，按每分四秒换成越野滑雪的出发延迟。这里说的是这种赛制，不是北欧两项的全部比赛；紧凑赛等赛制另有安排。同样，比赛以第一个冲线结束，而不是以一堆异质的子分数的最终加总结束。

edits.before: 这个对比揭示了终点线的一个好处，一个抽象分数永远没有的好处。终点线上发生的事情是一个物理事实，谁的躯干先到达那个垂直平面，这件事一旦发生就无法更改，不依赖任何后来的换算。而一个抽象的总分不是物理事实，它是一次计算的结果，而计算是可以重做的。把胜负系于一个物理事实，胜负就被锁死在了那一刻;把胜负系于一个计算，胜负就永远暴露在重新计算的可能之下。十项全能选择了后者，于是它的每一个历史结论都是可修改的。
edits.after: 这个对比揭示了终点线的一个好处，一个抽象分数永远没有的好处。终点线上发生的事情是一个物理事实，谁的躯干先到达那个垂直平面，这件事一旦发生就无法更改，不依赖任何后来的换算。而一个抽象的总分不是物理事实，它是一次计算的结果，而计算是可以重做的。把最后的比较落在终点线上，后来换算表的改变不会改变当时谁先冲线；当然，正式结果仍可能涉及犯规等裁决。十项全能则还多一层：即使十个原始成绩不动，换一张表也能算出不同的比较总分。可重算的是这种比较，不是说每一届正式胜负都随新表自动重写。

edits.before:
One competition, several totals

Jim Thorpe's 1912 decathlon can be assigned different totals under different historical scoring tables. Nothing about his ten performances changes. The number changes because the function that translates them into points changes.

This is the defining problem of combined events. Seconds, centimetres, and metres cannot be added directly. A decathlon must manufacture a common currency from ten unlike performances. The overall winner is therefore never produced by measurement alone. Measurement supplies ten inputs; a table decides their exchange rates.

A table is a model

Modern scoring formulas look objective because they are mathematical. For track events, points rise as times fall; for jumps and throws, they rise as distances increase. Constants shape the curve for each event. Once published, the formula gives every athlete the same treatment.

Fair application does not make the constants inevitable. They reflect historical performance distributions, normative judgments about balance, and expectations about what improvement should be worth. A table can be internally precise while its architecture remains a choice.

Early systems often used linear relations or event records as anchors. Later revisions introduced curved functions so that exceptional performances would receive differently scaled rewards. Each redesign attempted to prevent one discipline from dominating, yet every solution created another distribution of incentives.

Rewriting the events

Change the table and one changes the decathlon without moving a hurdle or redrawing a runway. A performance profile built around sprinting may gain relative to one built around throwing; an incremental improvement near one part of a curve may be worth more than the same percentage change elsewhere.

This affects training. Athletes and coaches allocate scarce time toward events where improvement is feasible and points are valuable. The table does not merely record a completed decathlon. It reaches backward into the preparation of bodies, encouraging some balances and discouraging others.

Curves do not remove judgment

A curved formula may track empirical performance better than a straight line, but it also hides judgment more effectively. The constants appear official, and official numbers acquire the aura of derivation. Yet published tables do not always provide a transparent genealogy explaining why each coefficient took exactly its value.

That opacity is not proof of arbitrariness. Committees can use extensive data and still fail to preserve a reader-facing chain from evidence to coefficient. The distinction is between a number having reasons and the institution making those reasons auditable.

There is more than one question

“Who is the best all-around athlete?” sounds like a single question. In practice it can mean at least three things: who accumulated the highest total under the current table; who performed furthest above the specialist norm in each event; or who displayed the most balanced profile. Those rankings need not coincide.

Other combined sports sometimes avoid a single synthetic total by counting places, head-to-head outcomes, or separate classifications. The decathlon chose a more ambitious construct. It promised that ten dimensions could become one ordered list.

A ledger that can rewrite its past

When tables change, historical performances can be rescored for comparison. That operation is useful and intellectually dangerous. It lets us ask how Thorpe would fare under a later system, but it cannot show how Thorpe would have trained if that later system had governed his competition. The counterfactual athlete is not contained in the old result sheet.

The scoring table is therefore both a bridge and an author. It makes incommensurable performances commensurable, then conceals the creative act behind a total. The total is real within the competition. What it cannot prove is that nature itself had already arranged ten events in precisely that order.

I. One Competition, Five Totals

Thorpe's ten performances in the 1912 Stockholm decathlon were these: 11.2 seconds in the hundred metres; 6.79 metres in the long jump; 12.89 metres in the shot put; 1.87 metres in the high jump; 52.2 seconds in the four hundred metres; 15.6 seconds in the 110-metre hurdles; 36.98 metres in the discus; 3.25 metres in the pole vault; 45.70 metres in the javelin; and 4 minutes 40.1 seconds in the fifteen hundred metres.

Those ten numbers have not changed in more than a century. They record what actually happened over those two days, measured by officials, entered in the record, and never subsequently altered.

What changed was the total score.

Under the 1912 table, those performances totalled 8,412.955 points.

Recalculated directly with the 1920 table's formulas, they yield approximately 7,751 points.

Looked up in the printed 1934 table, approximately 6,972.

Looked up in the 1950 table, approximately 6,267.

Calculated with the current formulas in the table used since 1985, 6,564.

The same competition, the same person, ten identical performances. The total falls from 8,412 to 6,267, then rises to 6,564. It loses more than two thousand points, then regains some.

Notice that the curve is not monotonic. It does not move steadily downward or upward, but descends to a trough before rising. This tells us that no single direction governs the rewriting of these tables: they become neither consistently stricter nor consistently more generous. The 1950 table is the least favourable to Thorpe; the current table treats him somewhat more kindly. Each has its own inclinations, with no continuous line connecting them. An athlete's historical score fluctuates through this directionless succession of revisions like a curve being moved by different hands in turn.

The athlete himself has done nothing. He is long dead, those two days long past. None of those ten runs, jumps, and throws can be repeated, nor need they be. What changed was not him, but the ruler used to calculate his total.

The preceding essay argued that every number the construct records is not the event itself, but an imprint left in the ledger after the event passes through a particular apparatus. Whether Hines's run is 9.9 or 9.95 depends on the cloth used to measure it. Here the issue takes a more radical form. A decathlon total depends not on which cloth measures one performance, but on which table converts ten unrelated performances onto the same numerical scale and then adds them together. And that table has been revised repeatedly. The five versions selected above illustrate those changes; they are not an exhaustive history.

First notice the numerical distance between the five totals: more than 2,100 points separate 8,412 from 6,267. This is not a gap between two athletes scored on the same table, so it cannot simply be translated into a difference in competitive ability. Nor does a decathlon ordinarily progress through qualification into a final. The point is that the same athlete's same performances acquire a different total when the scale changes. Nothing has been performed again, yet the number in the ledger has shifted dramatically.

II. A Table, Not a Measurement

We must first be clear about what this table is.

It is not a natural measurement waiting to be discovered. It is an apparatus constructed by a governing institution to define equivalences between different events. Nature provides no answer to the question of how much faster running counts as equivalent to jumping how many centimetres farther. There is no exchange rate between the hundred metres and the long jump. The table stipulates one.

The official history clearly records repeated committee work, congress adoption, and the replacement of one scheme of equivalences by another. In Prague in 1983, a working group explicitly treated the table as something to be redesigned according to policy objectives, including comparability, applicability at different levels, and future stability.

Its makers, in other words, have never treated the table as a truth, but as a tool. Tools serve purposes. When the purpose changes, or the understanding of it changes, the tool is remade.

In the official record, revision has at least four different meanings.

First, changing the benchmark performances to which scores are anchored. Which performance counts as a thousand points can change.

Second, changing the mathematical form of the conversion. The function relating performance to points can be linear, progressive, strongly progressive, or curved in different directions for different events.

Third, changing whether the table serves only combined events or also general comparisons between disciplines.

Fourth, changing the direction and strength of progression. How many points a fixed improvement earns at a low level, and how many at a high level, can be adjusted.

Each of these four meanings offers an opportunity for rewriting. The table has used them all.

Consider them together and something becomes apparent: almost no part of this table is immovable. Its benchmark performances, mathematical shape, scope, and direction of progression can all change. What remains fixed? Only the shell: converting ten events into points and adding them. Every specific element within that framework is an adjustable parameter. Something whose anchors, shape, scope, and direction can all be altered can hardly be said to measure an objective quantity. It looks more like a convention that can be repeatedly reconfigured.

A popular simplification says decathlon points were settled once and for all in 1912, when someone decided what they should be. This is misleading. Official records show successive institutional rewritings in 1920–21, 1934, 1950–52, 1962, and 1984, followed by several limited adjustments to the tables.

As for who compiled the original 1912 table, no definite answer is available. The accessible formula sheet explains its method and benchmarks but does not reliably identify a sole compiler. Later official histories describe proposals by the organisers, consultation with experts, and the eventual adoption of a linear table. The safest account is that the Stockholm organisers made the initial proposal, consulted experts, and arrived at an adopted linear table. Available primary sources do not justify confidently attributing authorship of the mathematics to one person.

This missing author is more revealing than it may seem. The table is the sport's central rule. It has determined the fate of every decathlete for more than a century, yet we cannot clearly say who first established it. By contrast, the names, performances, and placings of the athletes it scores are all recorded meticulously. The construct records its objects of measurement with extraordinary precision, but records the basis of its own measuring ambiguously. This asymmetry recurs throughout the series. It is especially striking here because what remains ambiguous is the ruler's own origin.

This is the same kind of gap encountered in preceding essays. A construct that demands evidence for every performance lacks sufficient evidence concerning the authorship of its most foundational table.

III. Every Revision Changes the Component Scores

The clearest way to see how the table changes is to hold an athlete's ten performances constant and vary the table. That is how Thorpe's five totals were produced. More revealing than the changing totals, however, are the changing component scores.

Under the 1912 table, Thorpe's 1.87-metre high jump earned 958 points, and his 15.6-second hurdles earned 943. Both were enormous scores under that table.

It is worth putting 958 high-jump points in perspective. The 1912 table assigned a thousand points to each event's 1908 Olympic record. Thorpe's 1.87 earning 958 meant that on this linear table it was already very close to the Olympic-record level of the time. The same 1.87 is worth only 687 today, not because the height has become lower, but because the benchmarks and conversion have changed. A height close to the Olympic record in 1912 is not thereby equally close to the record today. What this comparison directly shows is that an unchanged height earns fewer points. On its own, it does not establish that high jumping has been devalued against every other event at every performance level.

Under the present table, those same two performances earn 687 for the high jump and 751 for the hurdles.

His pole vault falls hardest. 3.25 metres earned 751.6 points in 1912; under the current formula it earns 418.

751 to 418. The same 3.25 metres. More than three hundred points lost, nearly half its value.

This is not a change in athletic performance but in the conversion apparatus. The 1912 table valued a 3.25-metre vault at about 750 points. The present table values it at just over four hundred. One table's valuation of the same vault is nearly twice the other's.

Which is right? There is no answer, because no objectively correct valuation awaits measurement here. How many points a 3.25-metre vault should earn depends on how much weight the table wants pole vaulting to carry within the ten events. That is a policy choice, not a fact.

There is a directional consequence worth noticing. Thorpe's total fell to its minimum of 6,267 under the 1950 table, then rose to 6,564 under the current one. Rewriting can raise historical performances as well as lower them.

There are other upward examples. C. K. Yang's Olympic silver-medal performance in 1960 is worth 8,010 under a later scoring system. Thompson's winning performance in 1984 earned 8,798 under the table then in force, while current statistical presentations give it 8,847. The same decathlon gains several dozen points when the table changes.

Rewriting therefore does not uniformly devalue the past or uniformly elevate it. It redistributes. Every revision reallocates the points available to the ten events. Applied to a particular historical performance, that redistribution may raise or lower the total depending on the athlete's strengths at the time.

In Thorpe's set of performances, the high jump and hurdles earn fewer points under the current table, and his total falls. A different combination of performances need not change in the same way: the result depends on the actual marks and both scoring curves, not simply on which event is an athlete's strength. Revising the table can therefore change the relative positions of different kinds of athletes in cross-era comparisons.

An unsettling implication follows. When an athlete's career ends, he believes he knows his place in history, because he has a total that can be compared with predecessors and successors. But that place is not fixed. Years later, if past marks are recalculated for cross-era comparison under a new table, his comparative score and those of other athletes may change. His position in that recalculated sequence can rise or fall; the medals and official results of the original event do not thereby change automatically. He cannot determine which scale a later comparison will use. He may no longer be alive. The number into which a lifetime's effort has been compressed is not his to secure. It lies in the hands of those who revise the table afterward.

IV. The Curves Keep Changing

These five tables differ not only in numerical values. Their shapes have changed fundamentally several times. Those changes record the construct's changing understanding of fairness.

The 1912 table was linear. Each event's 1908 Olympic record was assigned a thousand points. Performances better or worse than it moved up or down from that benchmark at a fixed slope.

What does linear mean? It means that, whatever your level, a fixed improvement earns the same additional points. Improving from very poor to slightly less poor earns as much as improving from very good to even better.

The 1920 table remained linear, merely replacing the 1908 benchmarks with the 1912 Olympic records, still worth a thousand points. The anchor changed, not the shape.

The 1934 table broke with linearity. It came from Finnish work, calculated by J. Ohls in 1931, used in Finland from 1932, and adopted by the IAAF in 1934. It was progressive, pursuing the principle that equally good performances in different disciplines should receive equal scores.

What does progressive mean? The higher the level, the more additional points a fixed improvement earns. A tiny advance at the top is worth much more than the same advance at a low level.

Why move from linear to progressive? Because people recognised that the difficulty of improvement increases with performance level at different rates in different disciplines, and linearity did not reflect this. Progression was an attempt to make points correspond more closely to actual difficulty.

The 1950–52 table retained that philosophy but intensified it considerably. A scoring-table committee was appointed in 1946, and the redesign was undertaken by Sweden's Holmér and Jörbeck. They raised the top of each table to fifteen hundred points, placed a key equivalence at thirteen hundred, and tried to replace some previous expert judgment with empirical curves, particularly curves of world-record running speeds.

A turning point appears here and deserves a pause. The 1962 table reacted against the excessive progression of the 1950–52 men's table. The new men's table adopted a principle already used in the women's tables: moderate progression in track events, moderate regression in field events.

Regression is the opposite of progression. Moderate regression in field events means that, as the level rises, a fixed additional improvement earns fewer points rather than more.

Within just thirty years, then, the construct offered three answers to the same question. Linearity says every step is worth the same. Progression says the higher step is worth more. The regression adopted for field events in 1962 says the higher step is worth less.

None of these answers is wrong, because the question is not factual but political: what does this sport want to reward? Evenly distributed all-round ability, or breakthroughs approaching the human limit in one discipline? Different answers produce differently shaped tables. The construct changed its position three times in thirty years. If past marks are recalculated under each policy, their totals and comparative order can change. That is distinct from revising the original competition results.

Here something general about the construct becomes visible. Many questions it faces appear technical, requiring a correct formula, but are actually questions of value, requiring a choice of position. There is a fundamental difference: technical questions have right and wrong answers; questions of value involve trade-offs. When a construct treats a question of value as technical, it searches for a correct formula. The search never ends, because no correct formula awaits discovery, only choices with different costs. One reason the decathlon table has been revised repeatedly is that it is searching for a correct answer that does not exist.

V. There Is More Than One Way Even to Ask What Someone Should Score

The table left by the 1984 revision still governs scoring today. Criticism of it exposes the deepest layer of the problem: there is no agreed answer even to how “fairness” should be defined.

The 1984 revision was the decisive modern rewriting. The working group said the new tables should serve combined events alone; comparable performances should earn comparable points; all events should be mildly progressive; and top world-class totals should remain broadly unchanged. The Los Angeles congress adopted the tables for use from 1985.

Notice the working group's definition of fairness. It did not define fairness as equal statistical rarity, equal training investment, or equal physiological cost. Its definition was more of a compromise: comparable performances should receive comparable scores; the table should work from beginners to elites; data from specialist athletes should inform the design, but no individual discipline should overwhelm the combined competition.

That compromise was subsequently criticised as having become unbalanced.

The strongest modern criticism says the 1984 table is now out of balance, not merely old. Some research argues that the system is inherently unstable, structurally favouring certain events, especially the long jump, 110-metre hurdles, and hundred metres, while undervaluing throws and the fifteen hundred metres. The deeper criticism is philosophical: equal points should represent genuinely comparable difficulty.

The difficulty is that “genuinely comparable difficulty” itself has several mutually incompatible meanings.

The main competing doctrines of fairness in the literature are these.

One is equal difficulty: performances equally difficult to achieve in different events should earn the same points.

Another is equal rarity: equally uncommon performances in different events should earn the same points.

Another is equal all-roundness: no event should systematically dominate the total, and scoring should reward breadth.

An older doctrine is an equal law of training, measured by consistency in the progression of training loads. Critics argue that linear or near-linear conversions violate it.

The literature does not converge on any one of these doctrines.

This is the essay's most important point. In preceding essays, a performance could not be causally disentangled, or a number depended on the cloth used to measure it. Those were still cases of a definite question without a definite answer. Here the difficulty goes further: the question itself is not unique. Equal difficulty and equal rarity are different standards that produce different tables. Equal all-roundness is a third; an equal law of training a fourth. Before calling a table fair or unfair, one must choose what fairness means. There is no higher standard that can adjudicate that choice.

This deserves fuller explanation, because it touches a root of the whole series. Measurement presupposes a definite object to be measured. Length can be measured because what length is is clear. But what combined events seek to measure, “all-round ability,” is itself unclear. Is it the average difficulty of ten events, the combined rarity of ten performances, or a balance without specialisation? These candidates differ, and none can be identified as the true all-round ability. The problem is therefore not insufficient accuracy of measurement. It is that the object being measured lacks a definition. The construct assigns precise scores to something ill-defined, and precision conceals the missing definition.

Thus the demand that equal points represent genuinely comparable difficulty sounds clear, but conceals an unanswered question: comparable in what sense? In 1984 the construct chose a compromise definition, not because it had found the correct answer, but because it had to select something workable among standards none of which could be proved.

“Had to select something workable” is the key to the entire table. The construct is not unaware of the different standards of fairness, nor incapable of argument. Its predicament is that whichever it chooses will appear unfair under another, yet it cannot decline to supply a table, because the decathlon cannot proceed unless a total can be calculated. It therefore does not find the correct answer. It picks, among options none of which stands securely, something people can just about accept and that permits the sport to continue. This is not failure. It is the only thing an operational construct can do when faced with an insoluble problem.

VI. The Coefficients Are Official; No One Can Fully Explain Their Origin

The current men's decathlon uses one form of formula for track events and another for field events. Both have sets of coefficients, and the result is rounded down to a whole number.

The coefficients are public. The three coefficients for every event are printed in the rules.

But there is no official derivation of how they were produced.

No published official derivation has been found that would allow someone to reconstruct every coefficient in the current 1984 system from the beginning. Later researchers repeatedly note the absence of a transparent derivation. The coefficients are official; the process that produced them remains largely opaque in the accessible literature and cannot be fully reverse-engineered.

To be clear, opacity does not necessarily imply deliberate concealment. More likely, a working group combined extensive performance data, expert opinions, and several principles, then arrived at the coefficients through repeated adjustments. That process may have lacked a clean logic expressible as a formula. It was an engineering exercise, not a derivation. Engineering can yield precise results without leaving a reproducible path. Intentional or not, however, the outcome is the same: the governing rule can be used, but cannot be traced to first principles.

This peculiar condition deserves separate attention.

Every number in a table governing the sport is public. Anyone can use it to calculate a score precise to the individual point. The public material located here does not allow the choice of those numbers to be reconstructed step by step. That does not establish that no complete account was ever written or that no one within the institution knew it. The remaining gap is between being able to execute a precise public rule and being able to retrace its development from the available public record.

This connects with Essay Three. Amateurism once defended itself by invoking an ancient past that did not exist, and the falsity of that past never diminished its force for a single day. Here the situation is similar but subtler: no fabricated origin of the scoring coefficients has been exposed here; a fully traceable derivation is missing from the public material available here. They still operate precisely, determine every decathlon's winner, and turn Thorpe's pole vault from roughly 750 points into roughly four hundred. A construct's rules can be indisputably exact while this essay cannot fully explain from those materials why these numbers, rather than others, were chosen.

Precision and justification are different things. The table is extraordinarily precise. Any score difference between two performances can be calculated without ambiguity. But precision does not mean these numbers have a traceable justification. It means only that, once the numbers are accepted, every subsequent calculation is unambiguous. The construct conceals its lack of grounding through precision, and users often mistake precision for justification.

VII. How Other Sports Work Around the Problem

The decathlon is not the only sport that must combine different events for comparison. Looking at how other sports handle the problem shows how distinctive its chosen path is.

Modern pentathlon does things differently. It still uses points in its earlier disciplines, but in the final laser run it converts the points gap into a starting-time gap. The leader starts first; pursuers start behind at a rate of one second per point. The competition therefore ends in a race whose finishing order directly determines the medals.

Individual Gundersen events in Nordic combined use a similar approach: each point of the ski-jumping deficit becomes four seconds of delayed cross-country start time. This describes that format, not all Nordic combined competitions; formats such as the Compact use different arrangements. Again, the competition ends with someone crossing the line first, rather than with a final sum of heterogeneous component scores.

At the level of competition results, triathlon largely avoids the decathlon's deepest commensurability problem. It does not convert swimming, cycling, and running into separate point units and add them. Athletes are ranked by their time and finishing order on one continuous course. The rules define a finisher as an athlete who completes the course and crosses the finish line, with results ordered by finishing time.

Together these three examples reveal a common feature. None allows heterogeneity to remain permanently in the form of points. Modern pentathlon and Nordic combined convert differences between disciplines into starting-time differences for a final pursuit, then let an actual race settle matters. Triathlon directly uses cumulative time. In all three, conversions ultimately flow into something everyone recognises: who crosses the line first.

The decathlon did not take this route.

The choice may well be historical accident rather than deliberate design. The decathlon originated before electronic timing and precise pursuit-race mechanisms. Converting performances into points and adding them was probably the only practical solution. By the time other sports developed the cleaner pursuit format, the decathlon had accumulated decades of point-scoring tradition, with a long succession of records and placings expressed as totals. Adopting a pursuit then would have meant abandoning that entire history. It retained points not because points were better, but because it had travelled too far down that road to turn back.

It leaves heterogeneity where it is, resolving it through a permanent abstract scale. Long jump and shot put are not converted into seconds within the same race. They become points that are added together, producing a sum that corresponds to no actual race.

The distinction is fundamental. In modern pentathlon, changing the conversion table alters who concedes how many seconds to whom in that competition's pursuit. Once the race ends, the table's work for that occasion is done. It does not retrospectively change the previous edition's champion, because that champion was the first person across the line in that particular pursuit. The fact is fixed.

The comparison reveals an advantage of the finish line that an abstract score can never possess. What happens at the line is a physical fact: whose torso first reaches that vertical plane. Once it has happened, it cannot be changed and depends on no subsequent conversion. An abstract total is not a physical fact but a calculation, and calculations can be repeated. A later conversion table does not change who crossed the line first, although official results can still involve rulings on infringements. The decathlon adds another layer: even with ten unchanged marks, a different table can produce a different comparative total. That comparison can be recalculated; it does not follow that every original official result is automatically rewritten.

In the decathlon, a revised table can be applied to the performances of past competitions. The comparison concerns not just who crossed a final line first, but a total calculated from ten marks. If past performances are fed into a new table, their comparative totals change. Thorpe's five totals are the outputs of different tables, not five successive official verdicts replacing the original one.

The decathlon's distinctive feature is therefore that the conversion table itself has become the sport's central constitutional object. Other sports treat conversion as a disposable instrument: use it once, then let the finish line decide. The decathlon turns conversion into a permanent ledger whose accounting rules can be rewritten. Rewriting them makes a parallel historical comparison possible; it does not automatically replace the official results established under the rules of each original event.

VIII. A Ledger That Can Be Rewritten Retrospectively

Let us bring the argument together.

The construct faces a genuinely insoluble problem. There is no exchange rate between the hundred metres and the long jump. This is not something temporarily undiscovered; it simply does not exist. Running fast and jumping far are different things, with no objective rate of exchange waiting in nature.

Yet the decathlon requires them to be added into a total. It must therefore invent an exchange rate. Invent, not discover.

The table is that invented exchange rate. Because it is invented, it can be reinvented. It has indeed been rewritten repeatedly, as the five selected versions show. Each reinvention changes a policy rather than correcting an error: this version rewards all-roundness, that one breakthroughs; this one values pole vaulting highly, that one less so.

Something shared with the whole series appears here. What the table seeks is closure: making ten incommensurable events commensurable in one comparable total. It succeeds. Any two decathlons can be ranked by their totals. Closure has been achieved.

The price is that this closure rests on a concealed choice. The total can be calculated because someone has assigned exchange rates to the ten events, and those rates are policy choices without an objective foundation. Closure depends on not asking why the rates take this particular form. Ask, and it becomes clear that they could be otherwise. If they were, every total, ranking, and history would be different.

Essay Five described one kind of remainder: the construct admitted a performance, then discovered that the number it recorded contained four inseparable things. Here the remainder is different. The construct calculates a precise total that depends on an exchange rate whose origin it cannot itself explain. The total is precise; the exchange rate arbitrary. The precise total rests on the arbitrary rate, while users see only precision, not the arbitrariness beneath it.

Look again at the nature of the ledger.

In Essay Two, the first thing the construct learned was how to add; it had never been taught to subtract. Here the situation grows more complicated. The decathlon ledger can not only receive additions but be recalculated retrospectively. Change the table and all past totals become new numbers without altering a single performance. This is a power not previously encountered: changing every conclusion without changing any original record.

The construct has chosen not to exercise this power fully. It has not recalculated every historical decathlon under the new table and legally substituted the new scores for the old. No congress record explicitly debating whether to do so was found in the available material. Actual practice introduced the new table in 1985, while historical accounts often retain original scores and also display an adjusted score under the current table.

This is parallel historical presentation, not complete legal replacement.

Thorpe's competition therefore carries two totals side by side today: 8,412.955, the original score under the 1912 table, and 6,564, the score under the present one. Neither is deleted. Both remain.

The two numbers tell different stories. 8,412 tells how extraordinary an all-round athlete Thorpe was within the understanding of 1912, approaching the Olympic standard of the time in almost every event. 6,564 tells what the same competition is worth under today's valuation. Neither story is false; they stand on different exchange rates. A later reader seeing only the two numbers cannot discover from the numbers themselves that the entire difference comes from the exchange rate, not the quality of the performances. Numbers conceal the rate and leave two apparently contradictory results.

These are again the parallel ledgers encountered in Essay Four, and the coexistence of hand and electronic readings in Essay Six. When the construct cannot make something singular, its solution is often not to choose one version but to preserve both side by side. One performance, two totals; one run, two readings; one event, two tables. What it cannot close becomes two adjacent columns.

This is perhaps the construct's most characteristic manoeuvre throughout the series. Genuine closure is impossible because what is to be closed has no unique answer. It therefore settles for listing several answers side by side and allowing them to coexist, rather than imposing a single one. That looks like honesty, an admission that it cannot establish one supreme authority. Yet it is also an evasion, leaving the judgment to those reading the ledger. The parallel columns are both where the construct acknowledges non-closure and where it transfers the burden of non-closure to others. Readers confronted with 8,412 beside 6,564 must decide which to trust. The construct need not decide.

Return to the ten numbers that have never changed.

11.2 in the hundred metres, 3.25 metres in the pole vault, 4 minutes 40.1 seconds in the fifteen hundred. These are things Thorpe actually did: accurate, verifiable, unchanged for more than a century. But the total that adds those ten things into one number has five different values under the five selected tables, while historical accounts may display both an original and a current-table total. What actually happened remains fixed; its valuation keeps changing. The construct can record precisely what someone did. It cannot settle once and for all how much each of those things is worth.

This observation extends across the seven essays so far. From the ancient list of names to record registration, eligibility boundaries, measurement, conversion between hand and electronic timing, and finally the table making ten things commensurable in one number, the construct's powers have continually grown. What it records becomes ever more precise and detailed. Yet one thing remains beyond it: a standard that requires no choice. Every valuation demands an unprovable prior decision: which performance is worth a thousand points, how much faster counts as equally good, which kind of fairness counts as fair. Once those decisions are made, everything afterward is supremely precise. But none of the decisions themselves has an objective foundation. The more precise the construct becomes, the more deeply it conceals the choice beneath it, until users imagine a fact lies there when there is only a decision once made.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 三十多年不是一个短的间隙。它跨过了整整一代运动员。在这三十多年里，一批又一批的跳高者站上助跑道，他们受规则允许去用背越式，却没有一个人这样跳。这不是因为他们不知道可以这样跳，背向翻过一根横杆是一个任何孩子都能想到的动作。他们不这样跳，是因为有一个他们比谁都清楚的理由，而这个理由不在规则本上，在横杆那一边的地面上。
edits.after: 三十多年不是一个短暂的空白，足够一代运动员走过赛场。在那些年月里，一批又一批跳高者站上助跑道，规则留出的背向过杆空间却没有很快变成普遍使用的技术。这不能证明从来没有人想到，也不能证明无人试过。要理解这种迟滞，着地的安全是一个重要条件，而不是关于所有人都为何不跳的完整答案。限制技术的东西，有时不写在规则书上，而铺在横杆另一边的地面。
edits.reason: Root review: preserve thirty-year/generation scene and ground image, but remove universal mental-state claims and a sole-cause explanation of delayed adoption. Regulatory space is not rapid diffusion; safe landings are important, not an exhaustive account.

edits.before: 前七篇讲的是这个构如何建立度量，如何登记，如何划线，如何把不可通约的东西通约。那些都是这个构说了什么，写了什么，规定了什么。这一篇要讲的是相反的东西:这个构没有说的那一部分。跳高规则从头到尾没有规定过一个人该怎么过杆，而恰恰是在这句没有写出来的空白里，技术的真正边界被别的东西划定了。
edits.after: 前七篇讲的是这个构如何建立度量，如何登记，如何划线，如何把不可通约的东西通约。那些都是这个构说了什么，写了什么，规定了什么。这一篇要讲的是相反的东西:这个构没有说的那一部分。现行跳高规则没有指定一种必须采用的过杆姿势，而恰恰是在这句没有写出来的空白里，技术的真正边界被别的东西划定了。
edits.reason: The same essay documents historical head-first/somersault restrictions. Existing five editions already limit to current mandatory style.

edits.before: 二 规则从来没说过怎么过杆
edits.after: 规则没有指定一种过杆姿势
edits.reason: Do not contradict documented earlier style restrictions.

edits.before: 所以在泡沫垫出现之前，背越式不是没有人想到，是想到了也活不下来。一个尝试背越式的人，会在第一次落地时就付出代价，而这个代价足以让他放弃，或者让他的教练禁止他。
edits.after: 所以在泡沫垫普及之前，问题不只是有没有人想到背向过杆，更是能不能把它安全、反复地练成一项技术。缺少足够缓冲，会大幅增加试错的风险，使运动员与教练更难持续尝试。这不表示每一次早期尝试都会造成伤亡，而是说，安全的落地区改变了这种技术能够被发展和推广的条件。
edits.reason: A safer landing surface matters; do not assert inevitable death/injury on the first attempt or an impossible historical counterfactual.

edits.before: 这个区别在别的领域也常常出现，值得记住。一样东西成为主流，可以有两种非常不同的原因:一种是它本身最好，一种是它最容易传播。这两种原因经常被混为一谈，因为主流的东西看起来总像是最好的，不然它怎么会成为主流。但成为主流和最好是两回事。最容易传播的东西会成为主流，哪怕它并不是最好的;而最好的东西如果难以传播，可能永远只属于少数人。背越式的胜出属于前一种，它成为主流靠的是易于传播，而不是对每个人都最好。看清这一点，才不会把主流误当成最优。
edits.after: 这个区别在别的领域也常常出现，值得记住。一样东西成为主流，既可能因为它在一些重要方面表现更好，也可能因为它更容易学习和传播；这些原因还可能共同起作用。主流与对每个人都最优，仍然是两回事。达佩纳的解释提醒我们，把背越式的普及只归给普遍的力学优越性，会漏掉学习经济。它支持传播条件的重要，却不要求我们把传播当作唯一原因。看清这一点，才不会把主流误当成最优。
edits.reason: Keep Dapena learnability explanation and distinction from universal optimality, without treating it as a uniquely identified cause.

edits.before: 这里出现了一个前后不一致。这个构在1936年取消了那条会挡住背越式的条款，却没有取消那条禁止翻筋斗的条款。为什么。因为在1936年，背越式还不存在，还没有人能靠它跳出成绩，所以取消那条挡住它的条款，在当时看来没有任何风险，只是清理一条显得多余的老规定。而翻筋斗过杆那条，是针对一个已经出现过的具体动作的，所以留着。
edits.after: 这里有一个需要解释的差别：1936年前后，挡住头先过杆的条款被取消，而关于翻筋斗的旧限制仍有自己的历史。仅从条文一删一留，不能确定当事人当时预见了什么、为什么认为某项风险可以接受。可以说的是，规则对不同动作的处理并不相同，而其中一次删除，后来为背向过杆留下了空间。
edits.reason: Different rule clauses changed differently; that result alone does not establish legislators motive or what they imagined.

edits.before: 也就是说，这个构在1936年放行背越式，不是因为它预见到并且接纳了背越式，恰恰相反，是因为它根本没有想到背越式会出现。它取消那条条款，是在清理一条它以为不再有用的旧规则。它无意中为一个三十多年后才出现的技术打开了门，而它当时并不知道自己打开了什么。
edits.after: 因此，说1936年前后的规则为背越式打开了门，是从后来发生的事情回看这次删除，不等于证明当事人已经预见并接纳了那项技术。无论删除出于什么具体理由，它都改变了此后运动员可以尝试的空间。一条旧限制撤去，可能产生超出当时讨论范围的后果。
