edits.before:
Permission without possibility

High-jump rules define the bar, take-off, attempts, and measurement. They do not prescribe a single technique. That silence made the Fosbury Flop legal—but legality alone did not make it possible.

For decades, landing areas were sand, sawdust, or other surfaces that rewarded feet-first techniques. A jumper could be formally free to cross the bar backward while remaining materially unable to land safely. The space permitted by rules was larger than the space permitted by the ground.

The rule that disappeared

Earlier formulations had constrained body order and prohibited particular movements. When a requirement that could have blocked a head-first or backward clearance disappeared in the 1930s, officials were not consciously welcoming a technique that would become famous three decades later. They were removing language that seemed unnecessary in the world they knew.

This is a recurrent feature of regulation. A rule can function as a door without its authors recognizing what lies behind it. Removing the rule opens a formal passage; only a later material change reveals what the passage can admit.

A changed landing pit

Dick Fosbury began experimenting as a teenager after struggling with conventional styles. His school had replaced a harsher landing area with a softer one. The new surface did not invent the Flop, but it reduced the cost of trial, error, and backward descent.

The distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions is essential. Foam made the movement practicable. Fosbury's curved approach, adjustments, persistence, and competitive success made a practicable movement into an elite technique. Material opened a field of possibility; a person realized one path through it.

Parallel discovery

Canadian jumper Debbie Brill developed a remarkably similar backward technique independently. Earlier athletes, including Bruce Quande, also experimented with backward clearances. Parallel invention weakens the myth of a single isolated flash of genius. When several people encounter related solutions after landing conditions change, the common environment becomes part of the explanation.

This does not make the inventors interchangeable. Many athletes had access to soft pits; few turned the opportunity into a durable method, and fewer still won an Olympic title with it. Possibility can be shared while realization remains individual.

The straddle was not mechanically refuted

The Flop is often described as simply superior physics. Its curved approach and arched clearance can indeed place the body's centre of mass favourably relative to the bar. But biomechanical analyses do not establish one universally optimal style for every athlete. Some accounts suggest that the older straddle could produce advantages for particular bodies and movement patterns.

The Flop also won because it was comparatively easy to teach and reproduce. That is a different claim from universal mechanical superiority. A technique may become dominant because it travels efficiently through schools, coaching systems, and generations. The most transmissible solution can become standard without being uniquely best for every body.

The boundary was on the material side

No authoritative record shows a formal international ban on the Flop itself. Anecdotes about officials or competitors considering it dangerous should not be confused with legislation. Once the older body-order restriction was gone, ordinary high-jump rules left style open.

The decisive boundary remained the landing surface. When foam pits spread, several independent experiments became repeatable, coachable, and safe enough to survive. Rule, matter, athlete, and pedagogy aligned.

That alignment eventually raised the event to Javier Sotomayor's 2.45 metres in 1993, a record that remained unbroken through the manuscript's 2025 data horizon. Innovation opened a new trajectory but did not abolish limits. A door can release a wave of improvement and still lead, eventually, to another wall.

I. The Rules Allowed It, Yet No One Jumped That Way

By the mid-1930s, the wording in the high-jump rules that said “the head must not cross the bar before the feet” had been removed.

Before that, some versions of the rules contained a provision that the head must not cross before the feet or be lower than the hips. It excluded any head-first or back-first movement. A person could not turn over the bar face upward, because the head would go first.

Around 1935–36, this additional requirement governing the order of body parts was removed. The principal technical requirement remaining was simply to take off from one foot.

From 1936, in other words, crossing the bar back-first was no longer prohibited by the rules.

Yet the Fosbury Flop did not become mainstream until after 1968, and did not truly dominate finals until 1980.

More than thirty years lay between.

More than thirty years is no short interval: a generation of athletes can pass through it. Year after year, jumpers stood on the approach, yet the room the rules left for a backward clearance did not quickly become a widely used technique. That does not establish that nobody imagined it or tried it. Safe landing conditions are an important part of understanding the delay, not an exhaustive account of every athlete’s reasons. What limits a technique may lie not in the rulebook but on the ground beyond the bar.

Those thirty years are the heart of this essay. The rules opened the door in 1936, but for more than three decades almost no one passed through it. Leading athletes continued to use the straddle until the late 1970s. Thirty years separated what the rules permitted from what actually happened.

That poses a question: if the rules were not the obstacle, what was?

The form of this question differs fundamentally from those of the first seven essays. They asked what consequences the construct's written rules produced, and what they left out. Their answers lay in rules and written provisions. This answer does not. Here the rules were silent: they neither obstructed nor encouraged the flop. They did nothing. To answer, we must look outside the rules, at what they neither mention nor govern, at conditions quietly at work in the material world. For the first time in this series, attention shifts from what the construct says to the vast expanse of what it does not say.

The first seven essays concerned how the construct establishes measurement, registers results, draws boundaries, and makes incommensurable things commensurable. All concerned what it says, writes, and stipulates. This essay addresses the opposite: what it leaves unsaid. Current high-jump rules do not prescribe one mandatory clearance style. In precisely that unwritten blank, something else set technique's actual boundary.

That something was not a rule. It was the landing place.

The Rules Do Not Prescribe One Clearance Style

First we must establish the high-jump rules, because this essay rests on the distinction between what they say and what they do not.

Current World Athletics rules still compress the event into a few essentials: the athlete must take off from one foot; a trial fails if the athlete's action causes the bar not to remain on its supports; and a trial fails if, before successfully clearing, any part of the body touches the ground or landing area beyond the vertical plane of the nearer edge of the bar. Add the familiar elimination after three consecutive failures, and specifications for the width and length of the approach and minimum dimensions of the landing area.

These are what the rules say.

What they do not say is equally important. They do not prescribe whether the jumper faces the bar, whether head or feet cross first, whether the body remains upright, whether the athlete lands on feet or hands, or whether the technique is scissors, roll, straddle, or flop. To paraphrase the Smithsonian's summary: no rule specifies how a high jumper must get over the bar.

The rules define the legality of take-off, whether the bar remains, whether the ground is touched, the number of attempts, and the dimensions of the facility. They do not define clearance style.

Whether this silence was intentional is difficult to determine today; it was more likely unintentional. Rules usually acquire a provision only when one is needed. For a long time, how someone cleared the bar did not need specifying, because there were few feasible methods and none caused a problem. The silence looks less like a carefully considered blank than an absence of any need to speak.

That accords with the construct's usual practice. As Essay Two argued, rules grow out of disputes. They cover ground already fought over and remain silent where no one has argued. For a long time no one disputed how to clear the bar, because the few feasible methods were unproblematic. So the rules stayed silent. This was not an intention to leave room for technique, but the absence of any trouble requiring speech at that point.

Intentional or not, the silence had a consequence. If the rules did not govern style, its boundary had to be set by something outside them. That something was neither abstract tradition nor athletes' imagination, but a very concrete material condition: what a person landed on after jumping.

A person can imagine any manner of clearing a bar. Whether they can actually jump that way depends on where they will fall afterward. The rules may allow a face-up turn over the bar, but if hard earth or sand lies beyond it, falling backward can injure the head and back. Permission is one thing; the body's ability to withstand landing is another. After 1936 these diverged: the rules had given clearance, but matter had not.

III. From Loose Earth to Foam

The landing place passed through a clear material sequence: loose earth and sand; sawdust, wood shavings, and low mats; bundles of foam rubber held in netting; then purpose-built deep foam landing areas.

Early high jumpers and pole vaulters landed in earth or sand. In the 1960s some university teams began placing bundles of foam rubber, secured in netting, in their landing pits. Current World Athletics rules formalise modern foam landing areas with explicit minimum dimensions.

Every step in this sequence changed one thing: how freely a person could abandon a controlled posture while falling.

On hard earth or sand, the athlete had to land feet-first or use a cushioning three-point landing to avoid injury. This restricted clearance to movements that could finish on the feet or in another controlled manner. Scissors worked because the jumper remained upright and landed feet-first. The straddle was just manageable because the athlete could turn sideways or cushion the landing with the arms. The flop was not: it finishes on the back and shoulders, and falling face upward into hard earth or sand causes injury.

We can make this more concrete. Someone landing back-first from two metres must absorb considerable impact. If the back, neck, and head take it, the risk is real. The feet are the part of the body best suited to landing impacts; the whole human lower limb is built to absorb them. The back and head are not. A feet-first landing is therefore not an aesthetic preference but the only safe choice on an uncushioned surface. The flop asks someone to relinquish that safe choice, and the price becomes affordable only once the ground grows soft.

Before foam mats became widespread, the question was not simply whether someone could imagine a backward clearance, but whether it could be practised safely and repeatedly as a technique. Inadequate cushioning raised the cost of experimentation and made sustained attempts harder for athletes and coaches. This does not mean every early attempt had to cause injury or death. It means a safer landing area changed the conditions under which the technique could develop and spread.

This material sequence unfolded in stages, not simultaneously worldwide. What can be established is that American universities began using bundled foam rubber in the late 1950s; American high schools began following in the early 1960s; and many other schools still used sawdust pits. No complete country-by-country or facility-by-facility census of the transition was found in the available material. What is clear is the staggered process: American universities first, then many American high schools, while poorer facilities or those slower to modernise lagged behind.

Today that material condition has become a written regulation rather than a local practice.

World Athletics explicitly requires high-jump landing areas at major competitions to measure at least six metres by four metres by 0.7 metres, alongside specifications for approach dimensions and slope. National rule diagrams similarly focus on mat condition, dimensions, and safe facility layout.

Pause on this. The rules do not stipulate how a person clears the bar, but specify in detail how large and thick the landing mat must be. Style is free; landing is regulated. The construct remains silent about style and extraordinarily specific about the landing surface. Yet that very surface determines which styles are physically feasible. By regulating it, the rules indirectly and effectively regulate style without mentioning style directly at all.

Such indirect regulation is more concealed and harder to see than direct regulation. If a rule explicitly banned the flop, everyone would know it was prohibited and could debate whether the ban was reasonable. When a landing-surface specification indirectly limits style, almost no one notices, because it appears merely to be a technical safety requirement unrelated to style. The provision never mentions style, yet marks its boundary. An effective constraint is often not written under the name of what it constrains. It hides inside an apparently unrelated provision.

This is the essay's central structure. Silence about style and specificity about facilities work together. Style is scarcely regulated, but a safe backward landing depends on whether the facility has completed the material transition. That is the clearest institutional expression of the argument.

IV. One Replaced Mat

Fosbury began experimenting with his new method in high school at sixteen, because the straddle left him unable to clear ordinary qualifying heights.

He moved from upright scissors toward a backward clearance. That movement became feasible because, after his junior-high years, Medford High School replaced its wood-chip pit with a softer landing surface.

That sentence contains the essay's most important fact.

Fosbury could develop the flop not because he was more imaginative than everyone else, or at least not only for that reason. His particular high school happened to change its landing surface at that particular time. Had Medford not changed it, or done so several years later, his first backward landing would have taken him into wood chips, which did not provide enough cushioning. His coach initially disapproved of the new method and stopped opposing it only when his results improved.

We must be very careful here, because this is precisely where the documentary evidence repeatedly warns against overstatement.

The replaced mat was a necessary condition for Fosbury's development of the flop, not a sufficient one. Other students at the same school did not invent it. Changing the mat made the flop possible; it did not make it happen automatically. Its emergence also depended on Fosbury's experiments, curved approach, adjustments to take-off, and relentless refinement as his performances improved.

The accurate formulation is therefore this: material conditions opened a space of possibility, while the athlete's discovery, coaches' adaptation, and the economics of learning the movement determined the speed of adoption and eventual dominance. The mat was the door; Fosbury was the person who walked through. An open door does not guarantee that someone will enter. A closed one stops even the most determined person.

The distinction needs repeating because both misreadings distort the story. One is the genius narrative: Fosbury invented the flop through imagination alone. It erases the mat, presenting something produced under material conditions as pure individual inspiration. The other is material determinism: once soft mats existed, the flop had to follow. It erases Fosbury, presenting something requiring human discovery and refinement as matter's automatic product. Each erases half. The accurate picture joins them: the mat made it possible; Fosbury made it actual.

His pre-1968 progression can be roughly reconstructed. In his first high-school year he could not consistently clear five feet. After changing his technique, he improved from 5 feet 3¾ inches to 6 feet 3¾ inches during high school. In his second university year he reached 6 feet 10 inches. He first cleared seven feet during the 1968 indoor season, then won the 1968 collegiate championship, the US trials, and the Olympic final, clearing 2.24 metres.

From failing at five feet to Olympic champion: that curve owes something to the replaced mat and something to the person who refused to quit. Neither can be omitted. Their mutual necessity is precisely why the outcome cannot be attributed to either alone.

Notice that Fosbury changed technique because he could not reach qualifying heights with the straddle. He did not first harbour an ambition to revolutionise the event and then invent the flop. The old technique first defeated him; with nowhere else to go, he tried something different. Much technical innovation happens this way, not as an embellishment by those at the top, but as a last gamble by those approaching elimination. Someone already successful with the straddle has little reason to risk changing. Someone failing with it has a motive to try what others dare not. That motive could become an actual experiment only after the landing surface had softened and reduced the cost of error.

V. Two People, the Same Movement, Neither Knowing the Other

Brill independently developed a very similar backward technique, called the Brill Bend.

She developed it as a child or young teenager on the family farm, where her father built a homemade foam landing area. The BC Sports Hall of Fame says she developed it independently, perhaps even slightly earlier. The Canadian Encyclopedia likewise treats her method as an independent development parallel to Fosbury's.

The best evidence concerning contact between them says they were unaware of each other during their respective development. The Hall of Fame account says the Brill Bend and Fosbury Flop first met in 1966, at a British Columbia–Oregon junior meet in Vancouver; until then neither knew of the other. This is the clearest evidence of genuinely parallel invention rather than mutual borrowing.

Parallel invention is powerful evidence here, and it is worth explaining why.

Had Fosbury alone invented the flop, it might have been an isolated stroke of genius, a unique mind appearing by chance. The genius narrative would attribute the technique to his singular imagination. Brill's existence dismantles that narrative. Two people unknown to one another arrived independently at nearly the same movement at nearly the same time.

When two people think of the same thing simultaneously, it usually suggests that its emergence was not accidental but prompted by shared conditions. What did Fosbury and Brill share? Not acquaintance: they did not know one another. Not a coach: they had different coaches. Each independently had a sufficiently soft landing surface. Fosbury's school replaced its mat; Brill's father built a foam area.

Parallel invention thus points directly to material conditions. When a material condition becomes available in several places at once, the possibility it opens can be independently discovered by different people. The flop was not one genius's exclusive property. In an era of spreading soft mats, it was something someone would eventually discover; Fosbury and Brill happened to be the first two.

An earlier figure must be added. Backward or backward-like clearances were attempted before Fosbury became famous at the Olympics. The strongest accessible example is Montana's Quande, photographed clearing the bar backward in 1963. Quande, however, never converted it into elite performance.

Whether Quande counts as the first flopper remains disputed in later writing. Evidence shows him using a backward technique before Fosbury's public fame, but no governing body formally adjudicated priority. Nor was Quande's movement the fully standardised, globally transmissible elite technique later associated with Fosbury and Brill.

We now have three people: Fosbury, Brill, Quande. Three strangers independently arrived at backward clearance. This further suggests that the movement was not one person's solitary creation but a possibility enabled by the era's landing conditions, encountered separately by several people. The difference lies in who refined it into a winning technique and who did not.

Quande also illustrates something else: encountering a possibility and realising it are different things. He encountered the flop, clearing backward in 1963 before Fosbury's public fame. But he did not refine it into a winning technique, leaving him a photograph, a footnote in history. Fosbury encountered the same possibility and spent years refining it into an Olympic-winning technique. Matter opened the door, several people stumbled through, and the person who brought what lay behind it before the world was the one willing to spend years perfecting it. Matter supplied the possibility; a person supplied the realisation.

VI. The Straddle Was Not Disproved

A familiar account says the flop replaced the straddle because it was mechanically superior, a better technique. This needs qualification.

Dapena's 1980 paper did show that the flop's curved approach, body lean, and arched clearance allow the jumper to position body mass advantageously relative to the bar. Its most famous mechanical benefit is real: the body can clear while its centre of mass passes at the bar's height or even below it.

But Dapena's later review also argued that the straddle had not been mechanically disproved. Some athletes can generate greater elevation with straddle mechanics, while others benefit from the flop's faster approach and weaker free-limb actions. He concluded that, on purely mechanical grounds, both techniques should still be used today. The straddle's disappearance is better explained by ease of learning than by universal inferiority.

This matters because it dismantles an overly simple causal account.

The flop dominates the event: that is a fact. But it does not dominate because it is mechanically optimal for every body and every movement profile. The literature offers no consensus on that. Many coaching and physics explanations present it as the superior clearance method because of centre-of-mass geometry and rotation from the curved approach. Dapena's review, however, explicitly resists the stronger claim that it is mechanically best for all bodies and movement types.

The more defensible claim is narrower: the flop became the universal elite standard in practice, but the literature has not unanimously established it as the single theoretically best solution for every athlete.

Why, then, did it win? Dapena's answer is learnability. The flop is easier to learn than the straddle. A beginner can acquire its basic movement sooner; a good straddle requires longer refinement. In a system training large numbers of athletes, the easier technique spreads naturally because it delivers results faster per unit of training investment.

This shifts the replacement of the straddle from a question of mechanical superiority to one of learning economics. The flop is not better for everyone. It is easier to teach and learn, and therefore spreads faster overall. The explanations refer to different things: one says the technique itself is superior; the other says it is more transmissible. The evidence more strongly supports the latter.

The distinction recurs elsewhere and is worth remembering. A method may become dominant because it performs better in important respects, because it is easier to learn and transmit, or through both mechanisms together. Dominance still differs from optimality for every person. Dapena’s account reminds us that attributing the flop’s spread solely to universal mechanical superiority overlooks learning economics. It supports the importance of transmission without requiring transmission to be the only cause. Seeing this prevents us from mistaking dominance for optimality.

The straddle's departure was accordingly a process, not a date. It could still win Olympic gold in 1972, when Tarmak cleared 2.23 metres, becoming the last male Olympic champion to use it. It could still set a world record in 1978, when Yashchenko cleared 2.35, becoming the last men's world-record holder using the straddle. Only by 1980 did the flop dominate finals. Fosbury's own retrospective figures say thirteen of the sixteen Olympic finalists that year used it; from 1972 to 2000, floppers won thirty-four of thirty-six Olympic medals.

The straddle was therefore not defeated by the flop, at least not mechanically. It gradually fell behind in the contest of transmission. Over decades, an easier-to-learn technique pushed a technique that was not necessarily worse out of competition.

Compare this with Essay Seven. There, rewriting the decathlon table made a technique more or less valuable according to the table's inclinations. Here there is no scoring table. High jump has a height, with no conversion. Yet selection still occurs, governed not by points but by learning economics. In a system cultivating many athletes, an easier technique naturally wins even if it is not mechanically superior. The common point is that a technique's rise and decline often depend less on its intrinsic quality than on its position within a system.

VII. The Rules Prepared a Boundary, Then Withdrew It

One further question about the flop requires allegations to be separated from rulings: did anyone try to ban it?

Later anecdotes sometimes suggest that rivals or officials may have wanted to prohibit it as dangerous. That is the allegation.

No original official legislative record was found in the available material showing World Athletics or the IAAF formally banning, or coming close to banning, the flop itself. The record shows that, once the old body-order provision disappeared, legality depended on ordinary high-jump rules and the landing area a particular facility happened to provide. That is the adjudicative record.

These must be kept apart. A wish to ban it may have existed at the level of anecdote. The formal records examined here do not show a ban on the flop. Rumours of a proposed ban do not establish an enacted prohibition; nor should an absence in the records examined be mistaken for an exhaustive search of every archive.

There is nevertheless a deeper point here, connecting with Essay Ten.

Early high-jump rules did contain a prohibition on “diving, somersaulting, or handspringing.” The construct thus did impose some early boundaries on clearance: it prohibited diving and somersaulting. It has not always left style alone. At certain times it regulated it.

The manner of regulation is revealing. It prohibited movements already attempted and considered problematic. People had tried somersaulting over the bar, so it was banned. The flop, meanwhile, was incidentally excluded by the broader provision that the head must not cross before the feet. Once that provision disappeared in 1936, the flop ceased to be prohibited.

A difference needs explaining: around 1936 the head-order restriction disappeared, while the older somersault restriction had its own history. The deletion of one clause and retention of another cannot by themselves establish what the decision-makers foresaw or why they considered a risk acceptable. What can be said is that rules treated movements differently, and that one deletion later left room for backward clearance.

Calling the change around 1936 an opening for the flop is a retrospective description of what followed. It does not prove that the decision-makers had foreseen and accepted the later technique. Whatever the deletion’s particular reasons, it changed the space in which athletes could experiment. Removing an old constraint can have consequences beyond the matters discussed at the time.

A construct often sees the practical consequences of a boundary only when someone crosses it. Wording removed around 1936 later left space for Fosbury and others to experiment; that does not tell us how the original decision-makers understood the change. Essay ten develops the point through a clearer case: after forward-somersault long jumping appeared, the organization prohibited it through a new rule.

Hold that thought, with its limits. A construct cannot write in advance for every possible technique, and new movements often expose the reach of older provisions. But rules need not be purely reactive: organizations can anticipate risks and set general conditions beforehand. The later emergence of the flop cannot tell us exactly what those removing a clause around 1936 expected. This case shows how rule wording can leave space for a technique not yet mature, with consequences that become clear only when someone crosses the boundary.

VIII. The Door Opened on the Material Side

Let us gather the argument.

Current high-jump rules do not prescribe one mandatory clearance style. This silence is not an oversight but the construct's normal condition: it speaks only when needed. Yet the silence has a consequence. If rules do not govern style, something beyond them must set its boundaries.

That something is the landing place.

The styles a person can practise repeatedly depend on how they can land safely. Hard earth and sand favour feet-first landings, while attempts to land on the back carry substantial risk; deep foam provides important cushioning. Even when rules prescribe no single style, facilities constrain how a technique can be developed. The crucial question is not only whether a movement is permitted, but whether the ground allows people to keep trying it safely.

That is the time gap between regulatory permission and widespread technique. The old restriction disappeared in the mid-1930s without immediately producing a common backward style. As softer landing areas reached more facilities in the 1960s, experiments by Fosbury, Brill and others matured; Olympic success in 1968 then brought the method before a much wider world. It was not an absolute absence of experiments for thirty years. A permitted possibility became transmissible technique through material conditions and human practice.

But we must preserve the qualification and not turn this into material determinism.

Material conditions opened a possibility without determining the outcome. A soft mat cannot perform a flop: Fosbury, Brill and other experimenters turned ideas into movements. Transmission also involved learnability, teaching and training, and success in competition. Matter opens a door; people enter; methods that can be learned and taught help others follow. These layers interact. The outcome cannot all be credited to one of them, nor does this history by itself establish the exact weight of every factor.

The precise formulation is this: once the written anti-diving wording disappeared, the remaining decisive boundary for a safe, repeatable, elite backward technique was the landing surface, a material condition largely external to formal style rules. Material change itself did not guarantee the flop's emergence. Independent invention, learnability, approach mechanics, and competitive success were also causes.

The remainder in this essay differs from those before it.

Earlier remainders were things the construct left outside its ledger: unlisted names, discarded readings, causes not yet adequately separated, unexplained exchange rates. Here the remainder is a field of possibility whose conditions were not yet fully in place. A backward clearance needed more than regulatory permission: it needed a safe enough landing area for bodies to experiment repeatedly and turn an idea into a technique. Softer landings spread, while athletes’ practice and competitive success helped the method travel. The point is not that nobody could execute it for thirty years. A permitted possibility became a route accessible to many through material conditions and human practice.

A possibility whose conditions are not yet in place may be discovered by different people in several places as those conditions change. It differs from an unlisted name: a name does not re-enter the ledger by itself, while a technical possibility may encounter new facilities and new experimenters. Fosbury, Brill and Quande remind us that similar material conditions can offer opportunities for parallel attempts. But an open door does not make an outcome emerge automatically. People still have to enter and develop the movement.

That gives this remainder a distinctive place in the series. Its appearance depends not only on someone having an idea but on where and how safely people can try it. Softer landings in several places supplied a shared condition for parallel exploration; different athletes developed the movement through their bodies, experience and practice. There is a connection worth investigating beyond three isolated coincidences, without turning it into a law that material change must release inventions in batches.

Finally, look at the record curve, which leads this essay far ahead.

Sotomayor cleared 2.45 metres in 1993. That men's world record still stands today. Subsequent annual bests declined: 2.42 in 1994, 2.40 in 1995, 2.39 in 1996, then generally fluctuating between 2.36 and 2.40. They briefly rose to 2.41 in 2013 and 2.43 in 2014 before retreating again: 2.37 in 2024 and 2.36 in 2025.

This is prolonged stagnation, not continuing exponential growth.

It occurs precisely in the event dominated by the flop, the technique regarded as mechanically optimal and most likely to keep pushing the limits. The material door opened, the flop emerged, and records rose until 2.45 in 1993. Then they stopped, unmoved for more than thirty years. The event in which technique supposedly serves as the engine has stalled for over three decades exactly where that engine should be most effective.

What this means is a question for Essay Twenty-Three. Here we leave only the observation: what pours through an opened door can eventually reach its end. When it does, the construct confronts a new question, one it has long avoided: just how fast, how high, and how far can a person go?

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 前一篇讲的是背越式如何取代俯卧式，一种技术把另一种挤出赛场，用了几十年。这一篇讲的是相反的事情。铅球的两种技术，滑步和旋转，并存了七十年，到今天也没有分出胜负。它们不是一个取代另一个，是一直并排着，在同一批比赛里，由不同的人使用，谁也没有把谁淘汰掉。
edits.after: 前一篇讲的是背越式如何取代俯卧式，一种技术把另一种挤出赛场，用了几十年。这一篇讲的是相反的事情。铅球的两种技术，滑步和旋转，并存了半个多世纪，到今天也没有分出胜负。它们不是一个取代另一个，是一直并排着，在同一批比赛里，由不同的人使用，谁也没有把谁淘汰掉。

edits.before: 前面几篇里，这个构一直在做判断:哪个成绩算数，哪个不算，谁有资格，谁没有，一个成绩值多少分。它一直在裁定。这一篇里，面对两种并存了七十年的技术，它没有裁定，也没有裁定的机制。世界田径的项目介绍页把铅球呈现为用滑步或者旋转，它的技术规则只为使用旋转技术的运动员澄清了犯规和无意触碰的问题。规则管的是合法和安全，不管优劣。两种技术都合法，而哪一种更好，规则一个字都没有说。

edits.after: 本篇所查的官方规则与项目介绍，并没有替运动员宣布一种普遍更优的技术。

Lead review addition: narrow universal historical assertion to official rules/event descriptions examined for this essay.

edits.before: 这个不说本身是一个值得注意的姿态。这个构完全有能力说话，它对无数别的事情都作过规定，从投掷圈的直径到球的重量到犯规的界定。它不是不会开口，是在这件事上选择了不开口。而它选择不开口的原因，不是宽容，是它没有依据可以开口。要说旋转比滑步好，得有一个尺度把两种技术放在上面比，而这个尺度不存在，因为两种技术不在同一条路上。这个构对成绩有尺度，对技术没有，于是它对成绩不停地裁定，对技术只能沉默。
edits.after: 这个不说本身是一个值得注意的姿态。构对投掷圈、球重与犯规有明确规定，也用距离比较每一次合法投掷。但一次投得更远，并不会自动给所有身体、训练条件和风险偏好排出同一份技术次序。这里不是完全没有比较尺度，而是成绩的尺度不能独自替每个运动员选择路线。规则持续裁定成绩，同时把相当一部分技术判断留给教练、研究和运动员本人。
edits.reason: Distance is a shared outcome scale. Rules do not prescribe an optimal technique for each athlete; this is not incommensurability or a proof of no objective comparison.

edits.before: 可是同一批研究，得出的结论恰恰相反。
edits.after: 可是采用率的变化，还不能单独回答力学上是否对所有人都更优。相关研究给出的图景，比这个流行趋势复杂。
edits.reason: Later paragraph explicitly reports Kato finding higher average performances for rotation; do not call all cited studies the exact opposite.

edits.before: 这个区分在很多地方都用得上，不限于铅球。一样东西流行，和一样东西正确，是两个需要分开的问题。流行的东西看起来总像是正确的，因为如果它不正确，怎么会有这么多人用。可是流行可以由许多和正确无关的原因造成:传播得快，学起来容易，或者仅仅因为已经有很多人在用而形成了跟随。把流行当作正确的证据，是一个很常见也很隐蔽的错误。铅球把这个错误暴露得特别清楚，因为这里恰好有一批人去测了两种技术的实际表现，结果发现越来越流行的那一种，并没有在成绩上真正胜出。
edits.after: 这个区分不限于铅球。流行可以反映真实优势，也可能受到教学、训练体系、先行者与跟随效应影响。所以采用率值得看，却不是关于每个人技术选择的最后判决。铅球的研究既有支持旋转在某些样本中取得更高成绩的结果，也有强调两种技术可以达到相近距离的分析。问题不在于把流行倒过来判成错误，而在于不让它替代具体比较。
edits.reason: Keep adoption versus suitability distinction, not a contrary all-results conclusion unsupported by heterogeneous studies.

edits.before: 这就是这项运动不坍缩成单一公式的意思。如果存在一套普遍最优的组合，那么所有顶尖选手最终都会趋近那套组合，两种技术里必有一种在所有三个要素上都不如另一种，于是被淘汰。可实际情况是，没有哪一种在所有要素上都占优。旋转用出手速度换取了角度和高度上的损失，滑步用角度和高度补偿了速度上的不足。这是一种权衡，不是一种碾压。
edits.after: 这说明，不能只看出手速度一个指标就判断技术优劣。速度、角度与高度需要共同作用，某个要素的优势可能被另一个要素抵消。但有权衡，不等于整体上永远没有更好的组合；一套最优方案也未必在三个要素上分别都占优。这里的证据较窄：这份比赛样本中的不同选手，通过不同参数组合取得了相近的距离。
edits.reason: An optimum for a scalar distance objective may trade release speed, angle and height; it need not dominate every component.

edits.before: 权衡和碾压的区别，是理解非收敛的钥匙。如果两种技术之间是碾压关系，即一种在所有决定成绩的要素上都不差于另一种，那么较差的那一种迟早会被淘汰，收敛就会发生。而如果是权衡关系，即每一种都在某些要素上占优，在另一些要素上吃亏，那么两种技术就会长期共存，因为你没有办法说哪一种整体上更好。铅球的两种技术恰好是权衡关系，旋转的速度优势被它的角度和高度劣势抵消，反之亦然。权衡关系是非收敛的温床，只要两种方案各擅胜场，它们就谁也淘汰不了谁。
edits.after: 权衡与全面压倒的区别，仍然是理解技术共存的钥匙。若一种方案在相关条件下各方面都不差，替换另一种的理由会很强；若各有所长，选择就更依赖个人怎样组合这些要素。但这既不保证两种技术会永久共存，也不证明未来不可能出现更好的方法。它说明的是：在现有这些比较里，不能仅凭某一个优势，就替所有运动员结束选择。
edits.reason: Trade-offs can explain coexistence without logically guaranteeing it or ruling out future superiority.

edits.before: 把这些放在一起，结论不是旋转赢了，也不是滑步赢了。结论是两种技术各有各的长处，各有各的代价，而这些长处和代价大致相抵，于是谁也压不倒谁。
edits.after: 把这些放在一起，不能说每一项证据都打成平手，也不能从某一项胜出直接推出人人都该改用同一种技术。两种方法的长处、代价与适用条件需要分别看。研究可以支持某种趋势，同时保留对具体运动员继续比较的理由。
edits.reason: Different studies/athletes/metrics do not establish a permanent population tie.

edits.before: 如果两种技术在成绩上打平，那么教练是怎么给一个具体的运动员选技术的。答案是，没有一个统一的办法。
edits.after: 两种技术都能取得高水平成绩，那么教练是怎么给一个具体的运动员选技术的。答案是，没有一个统一的办法。
edits.reason: Do not assume exact equality that research has not established.

edits.before: 这个对照能说明一件更一般的事:同一个因素，在不同的结构里会起完全不同的作用。易学性在跳高里是决定性的，因为跳高的技术之间存在优劣，易学的那一种一旦不更差就会全面胜出。易学性在铅球里只是过渡性的，因为铅球的技术之间是权衡，易学只帮助初学者起步，不决定精英的最终选择。所以不能笼统地说易学性重要或者不重要，要看它落在一个收敛的结构里还是一个非收敛的结构里。在前者它是终点，在后者它只是起点。同一个因素的分量，由它所在的结构决定。
edits.after: 这个对照能说明一件更一般的事：同一个因素，在不同的结构里会起不同作用。跳高里，较易学习与传播是解释背越式成为精英标准的一条重要线索，但这不等于证明它对所有身体都力学最优。铅球里，滑步的入门优势也不决定精英选手的最终方法。易学性不是一个到处产生同一结果的按钮；它要与身体、训练、资源和成绩上的实际表现一起发生作用。一个因素的分量，由它所在的结构共同决定。
edits.reason: EP08 explicitly denies proven universal mechanical superiority of the flop. Preserve context-dependent role of learning without contradicting it.

edits.before: 这两个项目合起来，说明了一件关于规则和技术的普遍的事。技术会不会收敛到一种，一部分取决于规则说不说话。规则保持沉默，技术就按它自己的逻辑走:如果存在一种普遍最优，技术会收敛到它，就像跳高；如果不存在，技术就一直分叉，就像铅球。而规则一旦开口，就直接决定了结果，把某些技术分支从可能性里删掉，就像标枪。
edits.after: 这两个项目合起来，说明规则会改变技术可以探索的空间。规则没有指定唯一动作，实践可能逐渐形成一个主流，也可能长期保留不同方法；其中还会有身体、材料、教学与训练的作用。不能把主流当作普遍最优已经被证明，也不能把分支当作不存在最优的证明。规则一旦明确禁止某类动作，则会直接删去一些本来可以探索的路线，标枪就是这里的对照。
edits.reason: Practical convergence does not prove universal optimum; branching does not prove none exists.

edits.before: 这也把前一篇和这一篇缝在了一起。两篇都是关于规则的沉默。前一篇里，规则的沉默让背越式最终取代了俯卧式，因为背后有一个物质条件在变，泡沫垫普及了，而背越式在软垫时代确实更容易学更容易扩散。这一篇里，规则的沉默让滑步和旋转一直不分胜负，因为背后没有一个普遍最优等着被收敛到。同样是沉默，结果不同，因为沉默只是把决定权交给了别的东西，而那个别的东西在两个项目里不一样。
edits.after: 这也把前一篇和这一篇缝在了一起。两篇都谈规则留出的空间。跳高里，落地条件、动作学习、运动员的实践与竞技成功共同推动背越式普及；铅球里，不同参数组合与训练路径让两种方法长期都有使用者。这里不需要先断言一个项目存在普遍最优、另一个不存在。同样的规则自由，可以在不同条件下形成不同的技术格局。
edits.reason: Keep two outcomes under similar rule freedom, without assuming their causal difference has been proved exhaustive.

edits.before: 可是面对滑步和旋转谁更优这个问题，它没有裁定，而且它没有裁定的依据。它没有一张表可以算出旋转比滑步好多少，因为这两种技术不是在同一个尺度上的两个刻度，是两条不同的路径，各自到达相近的终点。它也不需要裁定，因为这个项目的规则只要求球飞得远，不要求球用哪种方式被投出。
edits.after: 可是面对滑步和旋转，比赛规则没有给出一项人人必须服从的技术排序。距离当然可以比较，技术效果也可以研究；困难在于不能只凭一张成绩表，就把特定选手和条件下的优势变成所有人的唯一方法。规则也不需要完成这件事，它要求合法投掷尽可能远，而不是要求每个人用同一条路线抵达。
edits.reason: Same-scale distance comparison exists; no mandated technique does not mean research comparison is impossible.

edits.before: 所以这里出现了一种前面没有出现过的东西。前面几篇的余项，是被这个构裁定到账外的东西，或者是它裁定不清的东西。这一篇的余项，是一个这个构根本不去裁定，也没有能力裁定的问题。哪种技术更优，不是被排除在账外，也不是账目对不上，是这个问题压根不在这个构的裁定范围里。这个构管成绩，不管成绩是怎么来的。
edits.after: 所以这里出现了一种前面没有出现过的余项。哪种技术适合这个人，不是一个被取消的成绩，也不是一处账目差错，而是距离排序本身没有回答的问题。比赛可以给出名次，却不必替每个身体与训练过程规定唯一道路。这个问题留在研究、教练与运动员不断尝试的关系里，而不是被一句规则最终判完。
edits.reason: Preserve construct remainder as information unrepresented by distance ranking, not impossible objective knowledge.

edits.before: 这句话是这一篇最凝练的地方，值得展开。这个构度量的是结果，不是过程。它测一个球飞了多远，不测这个球是被怎样投出去的。出手的姿势，穿过投掷圈的路线，身体的转动方式，这些属于过程，而过程不进入账本。账本只有一栏，写着距离。于是一个必然的后果是，凡是只关于过程，不改变结果的差异，这个构都无从记录，也无从裁定。滑步和旋转的差别，恰恰是一个过程上的差别，两条不同的路通向相近的距离。这个构看得见那个距离，看不见那两条路的分别，更说不出哪条路更对。它的度量精确地停在结果那里，而过程从它的视野里整个漏了出去。
edits.after: 这句话值得展开。成绩表上的距离栏记录球飞了多远，不会单独展开这次投掷怎样被身体、训练与技术共同做出来。过程并非完全不受规则约束，技术研究也可以记录它；只是成绩排序不等于过程的全部说明。两个人投到相近距离，可能经过很不相同的路线。表里的数比较清楚，表外关于具体方法的判断却仍需继续。
edits.reason: Rules do regulate legal action; a distance column alone omits the whole process. Avoid claiming the institution literally cannot observe/record processes.

edits.before: 而这个不去裁定，恰恰暴露了这个构的一个边界。它想要的是收敛，是一个最优，是把一件事定于一尊。它对成绩就是这样做的，一个项目只有一条世界纪录线，最高的那个数就是纪录。可是对技术，它做不到，因为技术的最优不存在，两种技术在成绩上打平。于是它只能让两种技术并排着，既不承认哪一个更好，也没有办法让它们合并成一个。
edits.after: 这个不去作技术终审的安排，暴露的是成绩尺度的边界。它能够用一条世界纪录线留下当前最远的一投，却不能把那个人的路线直接规定成所有人的最优路线。两种技术在一些比赛中接近，在另一些样本或指标上又有差别。把它们继续留在场上，不需要先证明最优永远不存在；只需要承认，现有规则与证据还没有替每个具体的人结束这个问题。
edits.reason: Research uncertainty and rule silence do not prove no optimum exists.

edits.before: 这就是构不可闭合在这一篇里的样子。前面几篇里，构闭合不了，是因为它想装进去的东西太大，或者太多，或者对不上。这一篇里，构闭合不了，是因为它想收敛的那个东西，根本没有一个唯一的答案可以收敛过去。滑步和旋转，是两条同样有效的路，通向同一个大致的高度。构没有办法在两条同样有效的路里选出唯一正确的那一条，因为那条唯一正确的路不存在。
edits.after: 这就是这一篇所说的构不可闭合。前面几篇的困难，是有些东西太大、太多或彼此对不上；这里的困难，是比赛给出的一个数，并不把有关技术与人的问题全部回答完。滑步与旋转都是已经做出高水平成绩的路线。它们不必先被证明永远等效，才有理由继续存在；构也不能仅凭一次排序，就宣布关于每一个人的技术判断从此结束。
edits.reason: Keep the nonclosure thesis as no final reduction from result to one universally correct route, not an unsupported theorem of permanent equality.

edits.before:
Two motions in one final

Elite shot-put competitions routinely place two visibly different techniques in the same ring. The glide moves the athlete across the circle in a largely linear sequence. The rotational technique turns through the circle, borrowing elements of discus movement to create speed.

Both obey the same implement specifications, circle, sector, and foul rules. Both seek the same outcome. Yet decades of training, measurement, and global competition have not reduced them to one universally dominant solution.

A shared record line

World-record progression passes through athletes using different techniques. The ledger contains one distance column and does not mark a philosophical break when the leading style changes. It treats technique as an internal means so long as the attempt remains within the event's definition.

That neutrality is powerful. It lets athletes adapt method to body. It also means that the record curve cannot reveal which part of an improvement came from strength, coaching, surface, technique, or the changing population of athletes who select into each method.

Why rotation gained ground

Rotational throwing can generate high release velocity and has become increasingly prominent among elite men. But it demands exact footwork, balance, and control inside a small circle. The glide can offer a shorter learning path, a stable delivery position, and advantages for athletes whose strengths fit a linear sequence.

Coaches therefore do not answer the choice by consulting one universal formula. They assess anthropometry, speed, mobility, temperament, injury history, training age, and the time available to rebuild a throw. Technique selection is a judgment about a particular athlete under particular constraints.

A champion can reopen the split

Ryan Crouser's technical variations illustrate how innovation can occur within an established branch rather than by replacing it. Changes in start, rhythm, and turning pattern create hybrid solutions that do not fit a tidy binary. The taxonomy “glide or spin” is useful, but the best performers continually produce intermediate forms.

This is what a living technical field looks like. Names stabilize broad families while practice keeps escaping them. A classification follows movement more slowly than movement evolves.

Why no single answer emerges

If the rules specified an exact movement, branches would disappear by prohibition. Because the rules specify boundaries and outcome instead, the open interior becomes an evolutionary space. Coaches test solutions, athletes embody different trade-offs, and competition selects without guaranteeing final convergence.

Selection in sport is not a clean laboratory process. Athletes cannot repeatedly restart their careers with new bodies and techniques. A method that may be theoretically superior after ten years of development can be irrational for a twenty-eight-year-old champion to adopt. Path dependence protects multiple schools.

The question without a referee

Officials can determine whether a throw is valid and how far it travelled. They cannot decide which technique is the “true” solution to shot put. That question belongs to coaching, biomechanics, and the athlete's own risk.

The coexistence of glide and rotation therefore resists a tempting theory of technical progress. More data, stronger competition, and one objective do not inevitably yield one form. When a construct leaves means open, difference is not temporary noise on the way to uniformity. Difference is one of the products of the rule.

I. Two Techniques in One Final

The men's shot-put final at the 2016 Rio Olympics.

Crouser won gold, Kovacs silver, Walsh bronze. All three used the rotational technique.

In the same final stood Majewski and Storl. Both used the glide.

The first three were spinners, yet two emblematic gliders remained in the final. This was not one technique replacing another, but two techniques standing beside the same throwing circle on the same day, competing for the same gold medal.

The previous essay concerned how the flop displaced the straddle, one technique pushing another out of competition over several decades. This essay concerns the opposite. The shot put's two techniques, glide and rotation, have coexisted for more than half a century without a final verdict. Neither has replaced the other. Different athletes continue to use them side by side in the same competitions, neither eliminating its rival.

Throughout, the construct has never declared which is better.

This must be established at the outset, because it is the greatest difference between this essay and the first eight. Whenever two things coexisted in those essays, the construct eventually tried to deal with them: choose one, assign each a domain, or invent a category to contain them. It was always acting. Here, two techniques have coexisted for more than half a century and the construct has not moved. No selection, no partition, no new category. It simply lets them coexist. Something ordinarily eager to adjudicate chooses not to adjudicate. That choice deserves examination.

Previously the construct kept making judgments: which performances count, who qualifies, how many points a performance is worth. Here, facing two techniques that have coexisted for more than half a century, it neither adjudicates nor possesses a mechanism for doing so. World Athletics' event guide presents shot putting as using either glide or rotation. Its technical rules merely clarify fouls and incidental contact for athletes using rotation. Rules govern legality and safety, not superiority. Both techniques are legal. As to which is better, the rules say nothing.

That silence is notable. The construct regulates circle dimensions, shot weight and fouls, and compares legal throws by distance. Yet a longer throw does not automatically rank techniques in the same order for every body, training situation and tolerance for risk. This is not an absence of any common scale. It is a limit on what the performance scale alone can decide for an individual. Rules keep adjudicating results while leaving much technical judgment to coaches, research and athletes themselves.

II. One Travels Straight, the Other Turns

First we must establish what these two techniques are, because their difference grounds everything that follows.

Before O'Brien, the standard men's technique was an older front-facing or sideways movement: the thrower leaned back on one leg, hopped forward, and pushed the shot.

O'Brien replaced it. He began facing the rear of the circle, turned approximately 180 degrees, and moved into the delivery position at the front. He won Olympic gold in 1952 and produced the first eighteen-metre performance in 1953. His method became the recognised model for later gliders.

The glide's basic mechanical conception is linear acceleration: a low movement across the circle, a rapid transition into the power position, then a long, tightly controlled final delivery. It emphasises preloading the rear leg, moving rapidly with minimal vertical displacement, and establishing a powerful front-side block at release.

Rotation differs. Official Olympic biographies credit Alekseyev with pioneering rotational shot putting and identify Baryshnikov as its first internationally prominent exponent. Baryshnikov was using it in the early 1970s. In 1976 he set an official world record of 22.00 metres and won Olympic bronze in Montreal.

Its mechanical attraction is a longer acceleration path and an opportunity to generate more linear and angular momentum before the final delivery. Rotation can allow greater pre-acceleration and a larger potential increase in shot velocity.

The fundamental difference is therefore this: the glide moves the athlete across the circle in a straight line; rotation turns the athlete through it like a discus thrower. The glide seeks controlled, stable force production. Rotation seeks a longer acceleration path and the possibility of a higher release speed.

A popular misconception needs clarification. Some accounts call O'Brien's innovation rotational because it included a 180-degree turn. This is understandable but mechanically misleading. Governing-body and coaching descriptions identify his movement as the glide, a linear style, not the later fully rotational technique. His half-turn was a bodily rotation within the glide, not the continuous turning of the rotational method. They must not be confused.

This is more than terminological fussiness. It determines the essay's chronology. If O'Brien's half-turn counts as rotation, rotation begins in 1952 and the two techniques appear almost simultaneously. In fact, more than twenty years separated O'Brien's glide from Baryshnikov's later rotation. The glide ruled alone for twenty years before rotation appeared. Confusing their beginnings makes the story of non-convergence unintelligible, turning it into two techniques running abreast from the outset rather than a challenger arriving after twenty years of dominance.

III. Two Techniques Occupy One Record Line

The official world-record holders show how the two techniques successively reached the sport's summit.

Before O'Brien, the record belonged to an earlier technical family. Rose, Hirschfeld, Kuck, Torrance, and finally Fuchs used pre-O'Brien methods belonging to neither glide nor rotation.

From 1953 to 1973, the official record line followed the glide. O'Brien, Long, Nieder, Matson, and Feuerbach all used versions developed from O'Brien's method. For approximately twenty years, the glide governed the sport's official performance frontier.

Then rotation arrived. Baryshnikov's 22.00 in 1976 was the first officially recognised rotational world record. Thereafter both techniques appeared along the record line: Beyer, Timmermann, and Andrei on the glide side; Baryshnikov, Barnes, and today's Crouser on the rotational side.

One individual requires separate treatment because he exposes an important distinction.

Oldfield threw 22.86 metres in 1975. The performance is central to rotational technique's history, but was not ratified as a world record because of his professional status.

This must be seen clearly. Oldfield was one of the two most conspicuous early promoters of rotation. He began experimenting with it in 1968 and subsequently popularised it in America. His 22.86 was astonishing at the time. Yet it could not enter the official record, not because of the technique or insufficient distance, but because he was a professional.

Essay Three examined the construct's admission boundary: before measurement comes the decision about whose performances may enter. Oldfield's throw fell outside it. He had made the movement, made the throw; the distance really happened. The ledger refused it because of his status.

At Oldfield, then, the adoption history of rotation diverges from official record progression. As a technique, rotation could already produce 22.86 in 1975. As an official record, it entered the ledger only with Baryshnikov's 1976 throw. These are different lines. What a technique can do and what the construct acknowledges it has done are different things. Oldfield stands precisely in the crack between them.

That crack has special significance here. A technique's actual capacity can become completely disconnected from its representation in the official ledger. From official records alone, rotation reached twenty-two metres only in 1976. In reality, a rotational thrower had reached 22.86 in 1975, but his status excluded him. The record line therefore does not faithfully chronicle technical development. It chronicles the eligible portion of that development. A technique may have travelled far outside the ledger before an eligible athlete repeats it and the ledger recognises that it has arrived.

Who invented rotation consequently has two not quite identical answers, depending on what “invention” means. Official Olympic reference sources credit Alekseyev and Baryshnikov with the internationally recognised competitive model. American coaching memory often gives Oldfield a major role as promoter and early demonstrator. These accounts do not wholly contradict each other, but neither do they make the same claim. Inventing something that can enter official records and inventing something that throws far but cannot enter them are already divided by the admission boundary.

This also makes priority more complicated than it appears. Ordinarily, “who invented it?” means who first did it. Within a construct possessing an admission boundary, invention splits into two kinds: first to do it, and first to be recognised as doing it. Oldfield may belong to the former, Baryshnikov to the latter. Whom history remembers depends on which meaning is used. Official records naturally favour the latter, recognising only what enters the ledger. Memory closer to what actually happened preserves the former. Neither memory is necessarily wrong. They stand on opposite sides of the admission line.

IV. Elite Athletes Are Moving Toward Rotation, But

Look only at elite men today and a clear impression emerges: athletes are moving toward rotation.

Coded data support that impression. Salinero and Del Coso's World Championships dataset found a sharp increase in rotational use across successive championships: from seven gliders among ten athletes in Paris in 2003 to none among twelve in Doha in 2019. Hatase and colleagues examined major-meet champions, finding rotation used by thirty-seven of sixty-four champions in the 2000s and fifty-two of sixty-four after 2011. In a 2021 sample of regional top-eight finishers, forty-six of forty-eight used rotation.

These numbers look like convergence, as though rotation were eliminating the glide and the sport were finally reaching a verdict.

But changing adoption cannot by itself answer whether one method is mechanically better for everyone. The research presents a more complicated picture than the popularity trend alone.

While documenting the collapse in glide usage, Salinero and Del Coso explicitly concluded that earlier mechanical analyses had not demonstrated a sufficiently clear advantage to justify exclusive use of rotation. Elite athletes are moving toward rotation: that is fact. Rotation has been proved mechanically superior: that is not. Athletes' choices and scientific conclusions separate here.

This separation is central and deserves a pause.

Increasing adoption by leading athletes is ordinarily treated as evidence that a technique is better. Athletes have the strongest incentive to choose optimally; if all are moving toward rotation, surely it is better? The reasoning feels natural, but contains a gap. Athletes can choose a technique for many reasons unrelated to absolute superiority: it is easier to teach; coaches know it better; training systems for it are more developed; or leading athletes around them already use it, creating a trend. Increasing adoption records the combined force of these causes, not technical quality alone.

The distinction extends beyond shot putting. Popularity can reflect genuine advantages while also responding to teaching systems, established practice and imitation. Adoption matters, but it is not the final verdict on every athlete’s choice. Shot-put research includes findings of higher rotational performances in some samples and analyses emphasizing that both methods can reach similar distances. The task is not to declare popularity wrong, but to prevent it from replacing a particular comparison.

And when researchers actually measure their mechanics, the findings are not one-sided.

V. An Event That Does Not Collapse into a Single Formula

A mechanical comparison from the men's shot put at the 2009 World Championships provides this essay's firmest evidence.

Gliders had a lower average release speed: 13.73 metres per second, against 13.90 for rotational throwers. Release speed is the principal determinant of distance. On that measure, rotation wins.

Yet gliders achieved a slightly greater average distance: 21.34 metres against 21.18.

Lower release speed, greater distance. How? Compensation through a steeper release angle and a higher release point. The same study recorded release-height differences of as much as 0.29 metres in the gliders' favour.

Together these numbers show something important. Shot-put distance depends on three elements: release speed, angle, and height. Rotation has the speed advantage; the glide has advantages in angle and height. Each is stronger in different respects, and those strengths compensate, leaving the final distances nearly equal.

This shows why release speed alone cannot settle the comparison. Speed, angle and height work together, and an advantage in one can be offset by another. But trade-offs do not prove that no combination can ever be better overall; an optimum need not dominate every separate component. The evidence here is narrower: different athletes in this competition sample reached similar distances through different combinations.

The distinction between a trade-off and across-the-board dominance remains important for understanding coexistence. A method no worse in any relevant respect would offer a strong reason for replacement; where advantages differ, choice depends more on how a particular athlete combines them. This guarantees neither permanent coexistence nor the impossibility of a better future method. It shows that, in these comparisons, one advantage alone cannot finish the choice for everyone.

The 2017 World Championships biomechanical report shows why simple body-type rules are dangerous. It noted that Kovacs, 1.81 metres tall, produced one of the highest release points in the field, 2.22 metres or 122 percent of his stature, and one of the steepest release angles, 39.9 degrees. The tallest athlete discussed had both a lower relative release height and a lower angle. Body size matters, but does not map one-to-one onto technique choice.

The scientific literature is divided, and that division is precisely what this essay records.

The case for rotation: Kato and colleagues analysed performances by 176 international-level male shot-putters from 2001 to 2022, finding higher averages for best performances and season's bests among rotational throwers. They concluded that rotation was superior in producing higher performances among recent international male athletes.

The case against convergence: Salinero and Del Coso argued that earlier kinetic and kinematic analyses had shown no clear rotational advantage over the glide, and that elite athletes could achieve similar distances with either technique.

More interestingly, Kato's own data favoured the glide on another dimension. Gliders maintained a significantly higher proportion of their season's best, 97.31 percent versus 96.42 percent. The authors interpreted this as better maintenance of consistent throwing actions across rounds. They found no significant difference in best performance as a percentage of season's best, or in foul rate.

Thus even data used to establish rotation's superiority also established greater consistency for the glide. Independent variability research supports the importance of consistency: some studies associate lower technical variability with longer distances. This also explains why some coaches still value the glide in an age crowded with spinners.

Taken together, the evidence does not make every metric a tie, nor does an advantage on one establish that everyone should change technique. Strengths, costs and conditions of use need separate attention. Research can support a general trend while preserving reasons to compare methods for a particular athlete.

VI. Coaches Have No Single Answer Either

If both techniques can produce high-level performances, how do coaches choose one for a particular athlete? There is no uniform method.

Peer-reviewed evidence has not firmly established that choice should be based primarily on body type. Successful rotational throwing has been demonstrated by athletes with widely differing physiques, and some current coaching material argues that athletes of every body type and strength level can rotate. Yet strong coaching traditions also hold that taller athletes with longer levers and greater static strength often suit the glide, while more rhythmic, agile athletes suit rotation. The literature does not converge on a scientific rule.

The most common practical teaching sequence begins with standing throws, often introducing the glide first because it is simpler and easier to stabilise, then testing natural rhythm and athletic ability before transferring some athletes to rotation. This is a coaching tendency, not a universal doctrine.

Within that tendency lies something connected to the previous essay. The glide is taught first because it is easier to stabilise. This relates to the learnability that helped the flop displace the straddle, but leads to the opposite outcome. In high jump, the easier-to-learn flop eventually pushed the straddle out. In shot put, the more readily stabilised glide has not eliminated rotation; rotation has instead become increasingly prevalent at elite level.

Why has learnability not produced the same landscape in both events? In high jump, learning and transmission, together with safer landings and competitive success, helped the flop become dominant; that does not prove it the only suitable method for every body. In shot put, both techniques have produced high-level performances and offer different training advantages. Coaches may start a beginner with the glide, then consider a switch if the athlete shows the rhythm and other capacities rotation needs. Learnability influences the entrance without deciding the elite athlete’s destination by itself.

The comparison illustrates a broader point: the same factor can work differently in different structures. In high jump, learnability and transmission help explain the flop’s emergence as the elite standard without proving it mechanically optimal for every body. In shot put, an introductory advantage for the glide likewise does not decide the elite athlete’s final method. Learnability is not a button producing the same outcome everywhere. It works alongside bodies, training, resources and actual performance. A factor’s weight depends on the structure containing it.

Shot-put coaches consequently have no consensus equivalent to “everyone should rotate” or “all tall athletes should glide.” The mainstream position is more conditional: choose the technique that gives that athlete the best repeatable release, considering coaching time, rhythm, strength profile, and tolerance for error.

This is an unusually honest position. It acknowledges that no universal answer exists: the answer depends on the particular person. That is precisely where the construct cannot achieve closure.

VII. Crouser Opens Another Gap Between the Techniques

Crouser, today's best shot putter, pushed the issue further with the technical development that media and coaches began calling the “Crouser Slide” in 2023.

Public reports describe a modification preserving rotational intent while changing his route across the circle. Rather than starting fully parallel to its rear baseline, he begins at roughly sixty degrees and steps across more directly. Crouser connected the change with seeking incremental distance after already dominating through conventional rotation. Public explanations describe not an abandonment of rotation for the glide, but a hybrid entry designed to create a more direct route and better timing into the power position.

One point must be clear. No official technical paper by Crouser or his coach standardises “Crouser Slide” as a formal biomechanical category. In public discussion it is primarily a coaching and media label, not a settled scientific classification. Some call it a slide; others a modified rotational entry.

It should therefore not be treated as a third technique. It is more like a new gap opened between glide and rotation: something belonging wholly to neither side, whose own classification remains unsettled.

This reinforces the essay's theme. If two techniques had converged on one optimum, today's best athlete should be perfecting that optimum rather than opening a new gap between them. Crouser's experiment shows that even at the sport's summit, the optimal route remains unsettled and the middle ground between established techniques remains worth exploring. Someone who has won everything through rotation still seeks a better route. That itself suggests the best route has not been found.

There is another implication concerning why exploration continues. Once an optimum is found, the rational course is for everyone to approach it rather than strike out elsewhere. Yet Crouser, already at the world's summit with existing technique, still searches between two mature methods. In his own judgment, neither has reached the ceiling. The best athlete still exploring is the strongest signal that the event remains unsettled. True convergence will arrive when all leading athletes use one technique and refine only its details. Shot putting is still far from that day.

The construct's response to the Crouser Slide is the same as its response to glide and rotation: none. It need not decide whether this is a new technique, whether it is superior, or whether it merits separate classification. It asks only whether the throw is legal, whether a foul occurred, and whether the shot landed in the valid sector. The route used to produce the throw, its name, and its advantages over other routes are questions the construct never asks.

VIII. Once the Rules Speak, the Branch Cannot Appear

Comparison with other throwing events reveals where shot putting's non-convergence comes from.

Official discus instruction describes a rotational throw of roughly one and a half turns. There is no enduring elite bifurcation equivalent to glide versus rotation.

Official hammer instruction likewise describes rotation, with three or four turns. Rules and official event instruction present no comparable long-standing contest between different technical families.

Javelin differs from shot, discus, and hammer: its rules actively constrain technique. World Athletics' technical rules prohibit athletes from turning completely around so their back faces the throwing arc before release.

That provision directly blocks the emergence of a rotational-versus-linear branching structure like shot putting's.

This is the essay's destination and deserves explanation. Javelin could conceivably develop a rotational method, turning to obtain a longer acceleration path as shot putters do. But the rules explicitly prohibit facing away from the throwing direction, and any rotational throw necessarily passes through that position. Once the rules speak, the rotational branch cannot emerge. Javelin has only one broad technical direction not because linear throwing is proved optimal, but because the rules prohibit alternatives.

Now place javelin beside shot put.

Shot-put rules mandate neither glide nor rotation. Both are legal, both have produced high-level performances, and they have coexisted for more than half a century. Javelin rules explicitly prohibit turning the back toward the throwing direction, removing the particular rotational route discussed here. That does not eliminate every other technical variation. The contrast is not between an eternal tie and an event without branches. It concerns how an explicit rule changes whether a particular path can be explored.

Together the events show how rules alter the space open to technical exploration. Without one prescribed movement, practice may develop a dominant method or retain several for a long time, through bodies, materials, teaching and training. Dominance does not prove universal optimality, and branching does not prove that no optimum exists. An explicit ban, however, directly removes some otherwise explorable routes. Javelin supplies that contrast here.

This links the two essays. Both concern space left open by rules. In high jump, landing conditions, learning, athletes’ practice and competitive success helped the flop spread; in shot put, different parameter combinations and training paths have sustained users of both methods. We need not first declare a universal optimum present in one event and absent in the other. Similar regulatory freedom can produce different technical landscapes under different conditions.

We can now describe regulatory silence more fully. Silence is not inaction but an act of yielding the decision. Remaining silent about technique effectively says: I will not govern this; other forces will decide. The rules do not control what those forces are. In high jump, material conditions and learning economics combine to produce convergence. In shot put, mechanical trade-offs produce non-convergence. The silence is the same; the delegated power falls to different forces and yields opposite results. Silence does not decide whether convergence occurs. It decides who decides.

IX. A Question Without an Adjudicator

Let us gather the argument.

The two techniques have coexisted for more than half a century. O’Brien introduced the glide in 1952; rotation developed during the 1960s and 1970s, with Baryshnikov and Oldfield important figures. Both still appeared in the 2016 Olympic final. Such long coexistence warrants serious attention to why different methods retain users. It does not guarantee that they can never converge, or declare their performance exactly equal in every period.

The official rules and event descriptions examined for this essay do not declare one technique universally superior for athletes.

On the narrow question of whether any official body has declared one shot-put technique better, the answer is no. No World Athletics, IOC, or equivalent institutional document doing so has been found. Official texts regulate legality and safety, not superiority. The event page describes shot putting as using glide or rotation; technical rules merely clarify fouls and incidental contact for rotational athletes.

This is the essay's core, and must be linked to the whole series.

Previously the construct constantly adjudicated. It used rules to determine which performances count, admission boundaries to determine who qualifies, and scoring tables to determine what a performance is worth. Every verdict had a basis: a rule, a table, a line. The construct continually judged.

The competition rules nevertheless supply no ranking of glide and rotation that every athlete must obey. Distances can be compared, and technical effects can be researched. The difficulty is converting an advantage for certain athletes under certain conditions into one method for everyone merely from a results table. Rules need not accomplish that task. They require legal throws to travel far, not every athlete to follow the same route.

A different remainder appears here. Which method suits this person is neither an annulled performance nor an accounting error. It is a question the ranking by distance has not answered. Competition can assign places without prescribing a single route for every body and training history. That question remains within continuing research, coaching and athletes’ experiments rather than receiving its final answer from a rule.

The point deserves expansion. The distance column records how far the shot travelled without unfolding how a body, training and technique together produced that throw. Process is not wholly unregulated, and technical research can record it. A ranking of outcomes is simply not a complete account of process. Two athletes reaching similar distances may have followed very different routes. The number in the table can be clear while judgment about a particular method continues beyond it.

Not issuing a final technical verdict reveals the performance scale’s boundary. A world-record progression can preserve the farthest throw without turning that athlete’s route into the optimum for everyone. The methods are close in some competitions and differ in other samples or metrics. Keeping both available does not require proof that no optimum can ever exist. It requires acknowledging that current rules and evidence have not ended the question for each particular person.

This is what non-closure means in this essay. Earlier difficulties concerned things too large, too numerous or mismatched. Here, the number supplied by competition does not answer every question about technique and the person. Glide and rotation have both produced high-level performances. They need not be proved eternally equivalent to retain a place, and one ranking cannot declare technical judgment finished for every athlete.

Return to the Rio final.

Crouser won gold by rotating. Storl stood on the same field using the glide. Two people, two techniques, one task: pushing a 7.26-kilogram shot as far as possible. Decades of training and research have changed many judgments without bringing every athlete to the same movement. The rules have not made that choice for every body either. The methods can stand side by side, submitting their throws to the same measure. Who throws farther this time is not the same question as how each athlete must throw from now on.

The construct can measure every throw to the centimetre. That number alone cannot tell each athlete how to throw next. Measuring an outcome is not the same as finishing judgment on every route to it.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

標準差零點零七不是說所有差值都被關在零點一五到零點二九之間。這兩個數只是平均值上下各一個標準差的位置，實際差值還可能落在外面。它說明的是，在這項研究的條件下，給每次手計時加上同一個平均數，並不會把每次誤差都消掉。至於一百米，零點一五秒足以在一場競爭激烈的比賽中分開金牌和遠離領獎台的成績；但這只是提醒我們小差距的重要，並不是把這項四十碼研究變成所有一百米計時的誤差界限。
把这个量放到具体的历史里就更清楚了。一整个百分之一秒时代，无数块金牌和银牌之间的差距不到零点一秒。而这里说的是，单单是这个换算常数对某一次具体计时的不确定，就可能达到零点一五秒。也就是说，如果两个手计时的成绩靠这个常数换算之后放在一起比，它们之间小于零点一五秒的差距，是没有意义的，因为换算本身的抖动就有这么大。这个常数能把两块布缝在一起，却缝不出这个精度以内的名次。
把这个问题放到具体的历史里就更清楚了。许多金牌和银牌之间的差距不到零点一秒，细小差距当然值得认真对待。但这项研究并不推出一个适用于所有一百米成绩的零点一五秒门槛。两个换算成绩之间的小差距能说明多少，还要看原始计时的条件、误差及两者是否可比；不能只凭这个平均常数就宣布名次已经精确到百分之一秒。这个常数能把两块布缝在一起，却不能仅凭一道缝保证细到百分之一秒的名次。
把這個問題放到具體的歷史里就更清楚了。許多金牌和銀牌之間的差距不到零點一秒，細小差距當然值得認真對待。但這項研究並不推出一個適用於所有一百米成績的零點一五秒門檻。兩個換算成績之間的小差距能說明多少，還要看原始計時的條件、誤差及兩者是否可比；不能只憑這個平均常數就宣佈名次已經精確到百分之一秒。這個常數能把兩塊布縫在一起，卻不能僅憑一道縫保證細到百分之一秒的名次。
所以这项研究说明的事情是这样:这个常数的平均值是可靠的，而它对个体是不可靠的。用它来描述一大批计时的整体倾向，它是准的;用它来修正某一次具体的计时，它可能差得很远，而且没有办法知道这一次差了多少。
所以这项研究至少说明：一种条件下测得的平均差，可以描述那组计时的整体倾向，却不能直接充当每一次计时的准确修正。若没有那次比赛更完整的独立记录，就不能仅凭平均数知道它究竟差了多少。这也不能反过来证明，另一年代、另一种计时布置里的常数已经得到全面验证。
所以這項研究至少說明：一種條件下測得的平均差，可以描述那組計時的整體傾向，卻不能直接充當每一次計時的準確修正。若沒有那次比賽更完整的獨立記錄，就不能僅憑平均數知道它究竟差了多少。這也不能反過來證明，另一年代、另一種計時佈置里的常數已經得到全面驗證。
为什么要这样。因为手计时本来就有一个系统性的偏差，人按表总是偏早启动，偏晚停止，所以手计时倾向于偏快。向上进位是对这个偏快倾向的一个粗糙的补偿。既然手计时偏快，那就在读数的时候只往慢里凑，不往快里凑。
为什么要这样。手计时会受到发令反应和终点判断的影响，某些研究和换算惯例所面对的是平均偏快的手计时。但不能把它解释成“偏早启动、偏晚停止”：那样反而会把用时记长。向上进位规定的是读数如何报出，只朝较慢的一侧取值；单凭这条规则，还不能断定它就是为某一种反应偏差设计的补偿。
為什麼要這樣。手計時會受到發令反應和終點判斷的影響，某些研究和換算慣例所面對的是平均偏快的手計時。但不能把它解釋成“偏早啓動、偏晚停止”：那樣反而會把用時記長。向上進位規定的是讀數如何報出，只朝較慢的一側取值；單憑這條規則，還不能斷定它就是為某一種反應偏差設計的補償。
于是手计时的成绩里，叠了两层调整。第一层是向上进位，把它往慢里凑。第二层是那个零点二四的常数，再往慢里加一截。两层都朝同一个方向，都在把手计时的数往电计时的数上靠。
在采用这类零点二四秒换算的场合，手计时的成绩里便叠了两层处理。第一层是向上进位，把它往慢里凑。第二层是那个零点二四的常数，再往慢里加一截。两层都朝同一个方向，都在把手计时的数往电计时的数上靠。
在採用這類零點二四秒換算的場合，手計時的成績里便疊了兩層處理。第一層是向上進位，把它往慢里湊。第二層是那個零點二四的常數，再往慢里加一截。兩層都朝同一個方向，都在把手計時的數往電計時的數上靠。
可查的国际田联规则要求全自动计时系统由发令枪自动启动，延迟恒定且小于一毫秒。也就是说，系统内部对时间的把握精细到毫秒级。然而公布出来的成绩，仍然按项目长度读到零点零一秒或者零点一秒。
可查的世界田联规则分别规定了全自动终点摄影的采样要求，以及发令信号与计时启动之间恒定且不超过一毫秒的延迟。这里的启动延迟不是系统分辨率，也不是整套测量的总误差；它们是不同的技术指标。然而公布出来的成绩，仍然按项目长度读到零点零一秒或者零点一秒。
可查的世界田聯規則分別規定了全自動終點攝影的採樣要求，以及發令信號與計時啓動之間恆定且不超過一毫秒的延遲。這裡的啓動延遲不是系統分辨率，也不是整套測量的總誤差；它們是不同的技術指標。然而公佈出來的成績，仍然按項目長度讀到零點零一秒或者零點一秒。

这个偏好不是偶然的，它和这个构的一个根本处境有关。抹掉一个已经记进账的数，需要一个权力，就是宣布过去记错了的权力。而这个构从第二篇里那句授权条文开始，拿到的一直是登记的权力，不是注销的权力。所以每当它需要改变账面的时候，它总是想办法把改变做成一次登记，而不是一次注销。扶正一个已经存在的数，是登记;把它提升为官方，是登记;让旧的那一列失去资格，是让一个类别自然过期，也不太像主动的注销。它绕开了它没有的那个权力。
这些做法呈现出一种偏好：改变账面时，尽量通过承认已有读数或调整类别资格来完成，而不是把变化都写成对旧账的否定。第二篇引的那句早期授权条文写的是登记；但不能仅凭那一句，就断定后来从未形成注销权限。扶正一个已经存在的数，是登记；把它提升为官方，是登记；让旧的那一列失去资格，则可以让整个类别退出现行比较。对这些例子，我们可以这样理解：改变账面不必每次都宣布过去记错了。这不等于已经证明机构没有别的权限。
這些做法呈現出一種偏好：改變賬面時，盡量通過承認已有讀數或調整類別資格來完成，而不是把變化都寫成對舊賬的否定。第二篇引的那句早期授權條文寫的是登記；但不能僅憑那一句，就斷定後來從未形成註銷權限。扶正一個已經存在的數，是登記；把它提升為官方，是登記；讓舊的那一列失去資格，則可以讓整個類別退出現行比較。對這些例子，我們可以這樣理解：改變賬面不必每次都宣佈過去記錯了。這不等於已經證明機構沒有別的權限。
九秒九和九秒九五，同一次奔跑的两个数。这个构最后选择了九秒九五，让手计时那个九秒九退到旧列表里，然后连那个旧列表一起，随着项目规则的变化慢慢失去资格。它选九秒九五，不是因为九秒九五更接近海因斯真正跑了多快，那个真正的数字没有人知道，连千分之一秒的机器测到的也只是它自己那套系统里的一个读数。它选九秒九五，是因为从某个时刻起，它决定以机器那块布为准。
九秒九和九秒九五，同一次奔跑的两个数。这个构最后选择了九秒九五，让手计时那个九秒九退到旧列表里，然后连那个旧列表一起，随着项目规则的变化慢慢失去资格。不能把这个选择说成已经取得了毫无误差的真实用时；机器给出的也是一套测量系统里的读数。但这并不否认全自动计时能够提高准确性。这里还有一个制度上的决定：从某个时刻起，哪一套测量结果被统一采用，作为正式比较的标准。
九秒九和九秒九五，同一次奔跑的兩個數。這個構最後選擇了九秒九五，讓手計時那個九秒九退到舊列表裡，然後連那個舊列表一起，隨著項目規則的變化慢慢失去資格。不能把這個選擇說成已經取得了毫無誤差的真實用時；機器給出的也是一套測量系統里的讀數。但這並不否認全自動計時能夠提高準確性。這裡還有一個制度上的決定：從某個時刻起，哪一套測量結果被統一採用，作為正式比較的標準。
